source.label: Coastal Engineering · Lecture slides (RWTH Aachen, Prof. Schüttrumpf)

questions.q: The lecture opens by separating two disciplines. How is Coastal Engineering defined there?
options: Part of civil engineering that preserves and protects shorelines, estuaries and coastal resources
The discipline developing equipment and techniques to explore the sea bed and its resources
The branch of oceanography that predicts sea states from meteorological data
The design of ships and floating platforms for operation in shallow water
questions.why: Coastal Engineering is defined as the part of civil engineering that preserves and protects shorelines, estuaries and coastal resources. The second option is the slide's definition of Ocean / Offshore Engineering, which the slide explicitly marks as ≠ Coastal Engineering.

questions.src: L1 · The Coasts of the World
questions.q: How does the lecture define the coastline?
options: The area between the seaward and the landward influence of waves
The mean high water line as surveyed in the national datum
The strip of land that lies below the 10 m elevation contour
The boundary of the territorial sea, 12 nautical miles offshore
questions.why: The coast is the transition between sea and land, and the coastline is defined as the area between the seaward and the landward influence of waves — a process-based definition, not a fixed survey line.

questions.src: L1 · The Coasts of the World
questions.q: Which country has the longest coastline in the world according to the slide?
options: Canada
Indonesia
Russia
Norway
questions.why: Canada is first, followed by Indonesia and Russia. The total length of the world's coasts is given only as a range — approx. 356,000 km to 1,634,701 km — because the measured length depends entirely on the resolution used (the coastline paradox).

questions.q: Complete the population figures for coastal areas.
questions.text: About {{}} million people live less than 10 m above sea level, {{}} % of the world's population live less than 300 km from a coast, and {{}} out of 21 megacities are coastal.
questions.why: 625 Mio. inhabitants below 10 m, 66 % within 300 km of the coast, 14 of 21 megacities on the coast, and a six-fold population increase in the last 70 years — the "coastal squeeze" slide uses these to show that vulnerability, not only the hazard, is changing.

questions.q: The lecture writes risk as R = P<sub>f</sub> · E(D). What are the units of the three terms?
options: P<sub>f</sub> in 1/a, E(D) in €, R in €/a
P<sub>f</sub> in €, E(D) in 1/a, R in €/a
P<sub>f</sub> dimensionless, E(D) in €/a, R in €
All three are dimensionless indices between 0 and 1
questions.why: Risk is the coastal hazard (probability of failure P<sub>f</sub>, in events per year) multiplied by the expected damage E(D) in €, giving a risk in €/a. Climate change alters P<sub>f</sub>, growing coastal population alters E(D) — both push R up.

questions.q: Which problems does the slide list under "change of the coastal environment"?
options: Coastal erosion
Salinity intrusion
Coastal pollution
Drainage
Loss of biodiversity
Loss of tidal range
questions.why: Erosion, salinity intrusion, pollution, drainage and loss of biodiversity are the five bullets. A loss of tidal range is not listed — tidal range changes are treated later, under estuary dynamics and fairway deepening.

questions.q: Name the three principles of a sustainable use of the coastal area.
questions.why: Interdisciplinarity, interregionality and intergenerationality. They follow from the fact that many users compete for the same coastal zone, so methods and models must cross disciplines, regions and generations.

questions.q: Coastal protection is presented as the sum of which two tasks?
options: Flood protection + erosion protection
Flood protection + navigation safety
Erosion protection + water quality management
Dike maintenance + beach nourishment
questions.why: Coastal protection = flood protection (keeping water out of the hinterland) + erosion protection (keeping the coast itself in place). The morphodynamics lecture repeats the same split.

questions.q: Sort the properties of grey (hard) coastal structures.
items: Decades of know-how on design, function and level of protection
Weakening of the structure with time, needing monitoring and maintenance
questions.why: Grey structures buy proven, immediate protection; they pay for it with environmental impact, rigidity against climate change and a maintenance burden — the Netherlands alone expect 1.6 bn €/a for adaptation until 2050 plus 1.2 bn €/a maintenance.

questions.q: Hinkel et al. (2014) estimate the global cost of coastal protection (investment and maintenance) in 2100 at…
options: US$ 12–71 billion
US$ 1.2–7.1 billion
US$ 120–710 billion
US$ 1.6 billion
questions.why: US$ 12–71 billion globally in 2100 (Hinkel et al., 2014). The 1.6 billion € figure on the same slide is the Dutch annual adaptation cost until 2050 (Kabat et al., 2009) — don't mix the two.

questions.q: Which advantages of nature-based solutions does the introduction list?
options: Sustainable and environment-friendly
Adaptable to climate change
Self-sustaining to a certain degree
Economical
Additional benefits beyond coastal protection (co-benefits)
Immediate full protective function from day one
questions.why: The five advantages are sustainability, adaptability, self-sustainment, economy and co-benefits. An immediate protective function is precisely what grey structures offer and nature-based solutions do not — they need time to establish.

questions.q: Which of these are named as ecosystem engineers in coastal areas?
options: Dune plants
Mangroves
Tidal marsh plants
Seagrasses
Coral reefs
Reef-forming bivalves
Burrowing crustaceans
Phytoplankton in the open ocean
questions.why: The list is: dune plants, mangroves, tidal marsh plants, seagrasses, kelps and other macrophytic plants, coral reefs, reef-forming bivalves, burrowing crustaceans and infauna. Open-ocean phytoplankton builds no habitat structure and is not on it.

questions.q: The overview scheme sorts the hydrodynamic input parameters into three columns. Assign each phenomenon.
questions.why: Water waves: sea state, seiches, tsunami. Water levels: tides, storm surges, "secular increase" (long-term sea level rise). Currents: tide-, sea-state- and density-driven. Together with wind they are the input parameters for both the design (destabilising) and the transport (coast-reshaping) parameters.

questions.q: Put the lectures of the course in the order given on the overview slide.
questions.why: The course works outward from the driving processes (waves → sea state → tides → estuaries → storm surges) to the structures loaded by them, then to the morphology they reshape, and finally to nature-based alternatives.

questions.src: L1 · The Ten Commandments for Coastal Protection (Massie, 1976)
questions.q: Several of the "ten commandments for coastal protection" are about your neighbour. What do they demand?
questions.answer: Love thy neighbour's beach as thine own (6); do not steal thy neighbour's property nor damage it by your own protection works (7); plan in cooperation with thy neighbour, and he with his, and so forth (8). The engineering content: coastal protection is a chain along the shore — any measure shifts erosion to the downdrift neighbour, so planning has to be coordinated along the whole coast.
questions.why: The joke slide encodes real principles: work with nature (3), avoid provoking it (4), plan for yourself and your neighbour (5–8), maintain what you built (9), and repair past sins with sand (10).

questions.q: Which set of challenges does the lecture name as the tasks of the hour for coastal protection?
options: Understanding change, sustainable coastal management, adaptive structures, life cycle engineering, nature-based solutions
Higher dikes, stronger concrete, more dredging, faster construction, lower cost
Satellite monitoring, AI forecasting, digital twins, automated dredgers, drone surveys
Retreat from the coast, relocation of megacities, abandonment of ports
questions.why: Climate adaptation is called "the task of the hour": understand the changes, manage the coast sustainably, build adaptive structures, think in life cycles (planning → production → maintenance → disposal) and use nature-based solutions.

questions.q: What distinguishes capillary waves?
options: They are governed by surface tension and stay below about 2 cm in height
They are governed by gravity and occur only in water deeper than 2 m
They are generated by ships and always break as plunging breakers
They are the shallow-water limit of the cnoidal wave theory
questions.why: Capillary waves are influenced by surface tension, not gravity, and have wave heights of less than 2 cm. They are the first ripples the wind raises on a smooth surface and the seed from which wind waves grow.

questions.q: Assign each symbol from the wave definition sketch to its meaning.
pairs: Deflection of the surface from the still water level
Water depth at the breaking point
questions.why: These symbols recur through the whole course. Note the distinction between h (water depth) and H (wave height), and between c (the celerity of the wave form) and u (the orbital velocity of the water particles).

questions.q: Complete the elementary relation between wave length, celerity and period.
questions.text: In one wave period the wave form travels exactly one wave length: L = {{}} · {{}} .
questions.why: L = c · T. Everything else in linear theory — dispersion, group velocity, shoaling — follows from adding how c itself depends on the water depth.

questions.q: Assign each wave theory to the conditions it is valid for.
questions.why: The CERC validity diagram plots H/gT² against h/gT². Linear theory occupies the low-steepness deep-water corner; Stokes extends it to steeper deep-water waves; cnoidal theory covers shallow water, and the solitary wave is its limiting case.

questions.q: Which assumptions does the derivation of linear wave theory make?
options: The flow is incompressible
The water depth h is constant
The waves are periodic
The bed is movable and erodes during the wave cycle
The wave steepness is arbitrarily large
questions.why: Incompressible flow, constant water depth and periodic waves. On that basis the Laplace potential equation Δφ = ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂z² = 0 can be used, and the small-amplitude (low steepness) assumption is what later allows the quadratic terms to be dropped.

questions.q: Which condition applies at the sea bed (z = −h) in linear wave theory?
options: ∂φ/∂z = 0, i.e. no flow through the bed (w = 0)
∂φ/∂t = 0, i.e. the potential is steady there
φ = 0, i.e. the potential vanishes at the bed
p = 0, i.e. the pressure is atmospheric at the bed
questions.why: The bed is impermeable, so the vertical velocity vanishes: ∂φ/∂z = 0 at z = −h. The other conditions are the kinematic and dynamic conditions at the free surface (z = 0) and the periodicity condition φ(x,z,t) = φ(x+L,z,t) = φ(x,z,t+T).

questions.q: The surface elevation of a progressive wave is η = a·cos(kx − ωt). What is it for a standing wave?
options: η = a · cos(kx) · cos(ωt)
η = a · cos(kx + ωt)
η = a · sin(kx − ωt)
η = a · cosh(k(h+z)) · cos(ωt)
questions.why: In the standing wave, space and time separate into a product: the nodes stay fixed and only the amplitude oscillates. Both progressive and standing waves satisfy the same boundary conditions — which is why a wall can turn one into the other.

questions.q: Complete the definitions used throughout the solution.
questions.text: Amplitude a = H / {{}} , angular frequency ω = 2π / {{}} , wave number k = 2π / {{}} .
questions.why: a = H/2, ω = 2π/T, k = 2π/L. The amplitude is half the wave height — a frequent slip when inserting H into the potential.

questions.q: Which expression is the dispersion relation of linear wave theory?
options: ω² = g·k·tanh(kh)
ω² = g·k·sinh(kh)
ω = g·k·tanh(kh)
ω² = g·h·tanh(kL)
questions.why: ω² = g·k·tanh(kh). It comes out of the kinematic surface condition ∂η/∂t = ∂φ/∂z at z = 0 and is the single relation tying period, wave length and water depth together. For kh → ∞ (tanh → 1) it gives the deep-water limit, for kh → 0 (tanh kh ≈ kh) the shallow-water limit c = √(gh).

questions.q: Rearranged, the dispersion relation gives the wave length in the transitional zone as…
options: L = (gT²/2π) · tanh(2πh/L)
L = (gT²/2π) · sinh(2πh/L)
L = (gT/2π) · tanh(2πh/L)
L = T · √(g·h)
questions.why: L = gT²/2π · tanh(2πh/L) — implicit in L, so it has to be iterated. With tanh → 1 it becomes the deep-water length L₀ = gT²/2π; with tanh(x) ≈ x it becomes the shallow-water length L = T√(gh).

questions.src: L2 · Influence of Deep Water Areas
questions.q: Sort each formula and criterion into its depth range.
questions.why: Deep water h/L > 1/2: the wave no longer feels the bed, c depends on the period alone (dispersive). Shallow water h/L < 1/20: c = √(gh) depends on depth alone (non-dispersive). In between, the full tanh formula is needed.

questions.q: Two swells with T = 8 s and T = 14 s travel across the deep ocean. Which arrives first, and why?
options: The 14 s swell, because in deep water c = gT/2π grows with the period
The 8 s swell, because shorter waves are steeper and therefore faster
Both together, because in deep water c = √(gh) is independent of the period
Cannot be decided without knowing the wave heights
questions.why: In deep water c = gT/2π, so longer-period waves run faster — the long swell outruns the short. This dispersion is why swell arriving from a distant storm sorts itself by period. Only in shallow water does c = √(gh) make all waves travel alike.

questions.q: In the linear orbital velocities, which hyperbolic functions appear?
options: u ∝ cosh k(h+z), w ∝ sinh k(h+z), both divided by sinh kh
u ∝ sinh k(h+z), w ∝ cosh k(h+z), both divided by cosh kh
Both components ∝ cosh k(h+z) / cosh kh
Both components ∝ tanh k(h+z) / tanh kh
questions.why: u = ∂φ/∂x = aω·cosh k(h+z)/sinh kh · cos(kx−ωt) and w = aω·sinh k(h+z)/sinh kh · sin(kx−ωt). At the bed (z = −h) sinh 0 = 0, so w vanishes while u does not — the orbits flatten into a to-and-fro motion that moves the sediment.

questions.q: The linear pressure formula p = −ρ<sub>w</sub>gz + ρ<sub>w</sub>ga·cosh k(h+z)/cosh kh · cos(kx−ωt) consists of which two parts?
options: A hydrostatic part and a dynamic (wave-induced) part
A capillary part and a gravitational part
A reflected part and a transmitted part
A steady part and a turbulent part
questions.why: It comes from the Bernoulli equation with the quadratic terms neglected: the first term is the hydrostatic pressure, the second the wave-induced dynamic pressure, which decays with depth through cosh k(h+z)/cosh kh.

questions.q: Complete the wave energy per unit surface area of a linear wave.
questions.why: E = ⅛·ρw·g·H². Energy scales with the square of the wave height — doubling H quadruples the energy, which is why design is so sensitive to Hs.

questions.q: How does the group velocity c<sub>g</sub> = n·c behave in the two depth limits?
options: Deep water c<sub>g</sub> = 0.5·c, shallow water c<sub>g</sub> = 1.0·c
Deep water c<sub>g</sub> = 1.0·c, shallow water c<sub>g</sub> = 0.5·c
c<sub>g</sub> = 0.5·c everywhere
c<sub>g</sub> = 2·c in deep water and c in shallow water
questions.why: c<sub>g</sub> = c/2·(1 + 2kh/sinh 2kh) = n·c, so n = 0.5 in deep water and n = 1.0 in shallow water. Energy travels at c<sub>g</sub>, not at c — the basis of the shoaling relation E·c<sub>g</sub> = const.

questions.q: A swell with T = 10 s travels in deep water. What are its wave length and celerity (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
options: L₀ ≈ 98 m, c₀ ≈ 9.8 m/s
L₀ ≈ 78 m, c₀ ≈ 7.8 m/s
questions.why: L₀ = gT²/2π = 9.81·100/6.283 = 156.1 m, and c₀ = L₀/T = gT/2π = 15.6 m/s. Useful rules of thumb in deep water: L₀ ≈ 1.56·T² and c₀ ≈ 1.56·T.

questions.q: A wave of T = 8 s (L₀ ≈ 100 m) reaches a location with h = 60 m. Which depth range applies?
options: Deep water, because h/L > 1/2
Transitional zone, because 1/20 < h/L < 1/2
Shallow water, because h/L < 1/20
Cannot be decided without the wave height
questions.why: h/L ≈ 60/100 = 0.6 > 0.5, so the wave does not feel the bed: c = gT/2π applies, the wave length is L₀, and neither shoaling nor refraction occurs yet.

questions.q: In shallow water at h = 4 m, how fast does a wave travel?
options: c ≈ 6.3 m/s, independent of the period
c ≈ 6.3 m/s, but only for T = 6 s
c ≈ 39 m/s, independent of the period
c ≈ 1.6 m/s, depending on the wave height
questions.why: c = √(g·h) = √(9.81·4) = 6.26 m/s. In shallow water the celerity depends on depth alone — the waves are non-dispersive, which is why a long swell and a short wind wave arrive together in the surf zone.

questions.q: A deep-water swell has T = 12 s. How fast does its energy travel?
options: About 9.4 m/s (c<sub>g</sub> = 0.5·c)
About 18.7 m/s (c<sub>g</sub> = c)
About 37.5 m/s (c<sub>g</sub> = 2·c)
About 3.1 m/s (c<sub>g</sub> = c/6)
questions.why: c = gT/2π = 18.7 m/s, and in deep water c<sub>g</sub> = 0.5·c = 9.4 m/s. A distant storm's energy therefore arrives at half the speed of the individual crests, which visibly overtake the group.

questions.q: How large is the wave energy per unit surface area for H = 4 m (ρ<sub>w</sub> = 1025 kg/m³)?
options: About 20 kJ/m²
About 5 kJ/m²
About 80 kJ/m²
About 160 kJ/m²
questions.why: E = ⅛·ρ<sub>w</sub>·g·H² = 0.125·1025·9.81·16 ≈ 20,100 J/m². Halving the wave height to 2 m would leave only about 5 kJ/m² — the quadratic dependence again.

questions.q: Which processes does the wave transformation lecture cover?
options: Wave breaking
Wave shoaling
Refraction
Diffraction
Reflection
White capping
Triad interactions
Tidal pumping
questions.why: Breaking, shoaling, refraction, diffraction, reflection, white capping and triad interactions — everything that changes a wave between deep water and the structure. Tidal pumping belongs to the tides/estuary lectures.

questions.q: Complete the breaking criteria.
questions.text: In deep water a wave breaks at a steepness of (H/L)<sub>gr</sub> = 1/{{}} . In shallow water the breaker index is H<sub>b</sub>/h<sub>b</sub> = {{}} .
questions.why: Deep water: H/L = 1/7. Transitional: (H/L)<sub>gr</sub> = 1/7 · tanh(2πh/L). Shallow water: the wave breaks when its height reaches about 0.78 of the local water depth — the rule of thumb that caps the design wave in front of a shallow foreshore.

questions.q: Which three breaker types does the lecture distinguish (from flattest to steepest slope)?
options: Spilling, plunging, surging
Spilling, collapsing, standing
Plunging, rolling, capillary
Surging, shoaling, refracting
questions.why: Spilling (gentle slope, foam spills down the crest), plunging (the crest curls over and plunges — the surfer's wave), surging (steep slope, the wave surges up the beach almost without breaking). The loads lecture adds "collapsing" between plunging and surging.

questions.q: Shoaling is derived from which conservation statement, for waves running perpendicular to the coast?
options: E · c<sub>g</sub> = n · c · E = constant (conservation of the energy flux)
E · c = constant (conservation of the energy density)
H · L = constant (conservation of the wave volume)
H / h = constant (conservation of the relative wave height)
questions.why: With θ = 0° no energy is lost sideways, so the energy flux E·c<sub>g</sub> stays constant. Since c<sub>g</sub> first falls as the wave enters shallower water, H must rise — the wave shoals. The shoaling coefficient is k<sub>S</sub> = H/H₀ = √(n₀c₀/(n·c)).

questions.q: Which law describes wave refraction, and whose principle explains it?
options: sin α₁ / sin α₂ = c₁ / c₂, explained by Huygens' principle
sin α₁ / sin α₂ = c₂ / c₁, explained by Bernoulli's principle
cos α₁ / cos α₂ = c₁ / c₂, explained by Stokes' principle
tan α₁ / tan α₂ = c₁ / c₂, explained by Shields' principle
questions.why: Snell's law in the form sin α₁/sin α₂ = c₁/c₂, explained by Huygens' principle (Christiaan Huygens, 1629–1695). Because c falls with depth, the crest turns towards the shallower side — wave crests become nearly parallel to the shoreline.

questions.q: How is the refraction coefficient k<sub>r</sub> defined from the wave ray spacing b and the angle α?
options: k<sub>r</sub> = √(b₁/b₂) = √(cos α₁ / cos α₂)
k<sub>r</sub> = b₂/b₁ = cos α₂ / cos α₁
k<sub>r</sub> = sin α₁ / sin α₂
k<sub>r</sub> = √(n₀c₀ / n·c)
questions.why: Because the wave rows stay parallel, b/cos α = const, so kr = √(b₁/b₂) = √(cos α₁/cos α₂). Where rays converge (b shrinks) the wave height grows — the reason headlands get the energy and bays get shelter. The last option is the shoaling coefficient kS.

questions.q: Sort each description to the transformation process it describes.
items: Crests bend because celerity changes with water depth
Crests turn parallel to the depth contours as they approach the beach
Energy spreads sideways into the sheltered area behind a breakwater tip
Wave heights decrease along the crest behind an obstacle without any depth change
Wave energy is returned by a steep, impermeable face
Superposition of incident and returned wave can produce a standing wave in front of a wall
questions.why: Refraction is driven by depth-dependent celerity, diffraction by a lateral energy gradient behind an obstacle (no depth change needed), reflection by an obstacle returning energy. All three act together in a harbour entrance.

questions.src: L3 · Natural Motion of the Sea
questions.q: How does the lecture get from a natural sea state to a regular wave?
options: Fourier analysis removes the directional spread (3D → 2D spectra), then statistical analysis of the irregular long-crested record yields the regular wave
The regular wave is measured directly and the natural sea state is derived from it by superposition
The natural sea state is averaged in space, which directly gives the regular wave height
Breaking removes the irregularity, so behind the surf zone the sea state is regular
questions.why: Natural sea state (short-crested, irregular) → Fourier analysis → neglecting the directional distribution gives a long-crested irregular sea state (2D spectra) → statistical analysis gives the regular, long-crested wave used in design.

questions.q: Assign each characteristic wave height its ratio to H<sub>s</sub> (Rayleigh distribution, N ≈ 1000 waves).
questions.why: These ratios follow from the single-parameter Rayleigh distribution. H<sub>max</sub> = √(ln N / 2)·H<sub>s</sub>, which gives 1.86·H<sub>s</sub> only for N ≈ 1000 — with more waves in the storm, the expected maximum grows.

questions.q: The cumulative distribution is P(H < H<sub>s</sub>) = 1 − exp(−2·(H/H<sub>s</sub>)²). What share of the waves therefore exceeds H<sub>s</sub>?
options: About 13.5 %
Exactly 33.3 %
About 50 %
About 1 %
questions.why: Inserting H = Hs gives P = 1 − e⁻² ≈ 0.865, so about 13.5 % of the waves are higher than the significant wave height. The 33.3 % on the same sketch is the definition of Hs as the mean of the highest third — not the exceedance probability.

questions.q: Complete the Rayleigh estimate of the maximum wave height in a record of N waves.
questions.text: H<sub>max</sub> = √( ln N / {{}} ) · H<sub>s</sub> , which for N ≈ 1000 waves gives H<sub>max</sub> = {{}} · H<sub>s</sub> .
questions.why: Hmax = √(ln N / 2)·Hs = 1.86·Hs for N = 1000. The maximum wave in a record is therefore a property of the record length as much as of the sea state.

questions.q: A dike toe stands in h = 5 m of water. Roughly which wave height can at most reach it?
options: About 3.9 m, because H<sub>b</sub> ≈ 0.78·h<sub>b</sub>
About 6.4 m, because H<sub>b</sub> ≈ 1.28·h<sub>b</sub>
About 5.0 m, because H<sub>b</sub> = h<sub>b</sub>
Any height — the breaker index limits only the period
questions.why: H<sub>b</sub> = 0.78·5 = 3.9 m. On a shallow foreshore the design wave is therefore capped by the water depth, not by the offshore sea state — which is why raising the design water level also raises the wave load.

questions.q: A deep-water wave has L = 70 m. From about which wave height does it break?
options: From about 10 m (H/L = 1/7)
From about 7 m (H/L = 1/10)
From about 3.5 m (H/L = 1/20)
It cannot break in deep water
questions.why: The deep-water limiting steepness is H/L = 1/7, so H ≈ 70/7 = 10 m. Deep-water breaking (white capping) is limited by steepness; shallow-water breaking by depth (Hb/hb = 0.78).

questions.q: Which transformation process makes wave crests turn parallel to the depth contours as they approach the shore?
questions.why: Refraction. Because the celerity falls with depth, the part of the crest in shallower water slows down and the crest turns — energy concentrates on headlands and spreads out in bays.

questions.q: Which process raises the wave height as a wave runs into shallower water perpendicular to the coast, without changing its direction?
questions.why: Shoaling. The energy flux E·c<sub>g</sub> stays constant while c<sub>g</sub> falls, so H must rise; the shoaling coefficient is k<sub>S</sub> = H/H₀ = √(n₀c₀/(n·c)).

questions.q: Who finally introduced the Beaufort scale, and when?
options: The British weather forecast service, in 1906
Sir Francis Beaufort himself, in 1806
Tycho Brahe, in 1590
The IAHR/PIANC working group, in 1986
questions.why: The scale goes back to Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) and Alexander Dalrymple, was shaped by Sir Francis Beaufort (1774–1857), but was introduced by the British weather forecast service only in 1906. (1986 is the IAHR/PIANC date for the zero-crossing definitions.)

questions.q: Assign each Beaufort number to its description.
pairs: Moderate breeze — small waves becoming longer, fairly frequent white horses
Gale / fresh gale — moderately high waves, crests break into spindrift
Strong / severe gale — high waves, dense foam streaks, spray affects visibility
Storm / whole gale — very high waves with long overhanging crests, sea takes a white appearance
Hurricane force — air filled with foam and spray, devastation on land
questions.why: Bft 9 matters for the definition of a storm surge: "severe wind" is set at u > 80 km/h, i.e. higher than Beaufort 9.

questions.q: What does the Douglas sea scale classify, in contrast to the Beaufort scale?
options: Wind sea and swell separately, i.e. the state of the sea rather than the wind
Only the wind speed, in finer steps than Beaufort
The breaker type on the beach
The tidal form factor of a location
questions.why: Beaufort grades the wind (with sea and land indicators); the Douglas scale grades the sea itself, and does so in two parts — wind sea (locally generated, still under the wind) and swell (long waves that have left their generating area).

questions.q: Sort the statements into the sea state they describe.
items: Long-crested, idealised, used in simple design calculations
H variable and T variable from wave to wave
Requires statistical or spectral parameters to be described
questions.why: The regular wave is the textbook idealisation; the natural sea state varies from wave to wave, which is why it must be condensed into H<sub>s</sub>/T<sub>Hs</sub> (time domain) or H<sub>m0</sub>/T<sub>p</sub> (frequency domain).

questions.q: Sort each item into the domain it belongs to.
questions.why: Both describe the same record. The time domain counts individual waves and averages them statistically; the frequency domain decomposes the record into its energy spectrum. H<sub>m0</sub> ≈ 1.05·H<sub>s</sub>, so the two wave heights are close but not identical.

questions.q: How is a single wave defined in the zero-crossing method (IAHR/PIANC 1986)?
options: The event between two successive passages of the water level through the mean water level in the same direction
The event between two successive crests of the record
The event between the highest and the lowest point of the record
The event between two successive passages through the mean level in opposite directions
questions.why: Same direction — hence the two variants, zero-up-crossing and zero-down-crossing. H<sub>i</sub> is then the vertical distance between the highest and lowest point within that interval and T<sub>i</sub> its duration.

questions.q: Who postulated the significant wave, and how is H<sub>s</sub> defined?
options: Sverdrup & Munk (1942) — the mean height of the highest 33.3 % of the waves in the record
Longuet-Higgins (1952) — the height exceeded by 33.3 % of the waves
Pierson & Moskowitz (1962) — the height belonging to the peak of the spectrum
Goda (2000) — the mean height of the highest 10 % of the waves
questions.why: Sverdrup & Munk (1942): "the significant wave with Hs and THs describes the irregular sea state statistically adequately". Hs = H1/3 is the mean of the highest third, not the height exceeded by a third. Longuet-Higgins (1952) later supplied the Rayleigh distribution.

questions.q: Why was H<sub>s</sub> defined as the mean of the highest third and not, say, as the mean of all waves?
options: Because it matches the height a trained observer estimates visually
Because the highest third carries exactly half of the wave energy
Because ships are designed for the highest third of the waves
Because only the highest third can be resolved by a wave buoy
questions.why: The significant wave height was intended to express mathematically what a "trained observer" reports — the eye weights the bigger waves. Walter Munk (1917–2019) developed it in the context of the Normandy landings of 6 June 1944.

questions.q: Why is the normal (Gaussian) distribution unsuitable for the statistics of wave heights?
options: H cannot grow arbitrarily high, because the wave breaks
The wave phases are interdependent
Negative wave heights are physically senseless
It needs two parameters instead of one
It cannot be integrated analytically
questions.why: The three reasons on the slide. The Rayleigh distribution instead is single-parametric (H<sub>s</sub> alone) and defined only for H ≥ 0 — needing two parameters is a property of the normal distribution, but not the reason it fails here.

questions.q: Who showed that measured wave heights follow a Rayleigh rather than a Gaussian distribution?
options: Longuet-Higgins (1952)
Sverdrup & Munk (1942)
Phillips (1958)
Kitaigorodskii (1973)
questions.why: Michael Selwyn Longuet-Higgins (1925–2016) in 1952. The key point is that the Rayleigh distribution is single-parametric: once H<sub>s</sub> is known, the whole height distribution follows.

questions.src: L4 · Statistical Distribution of Wave Periods
questions.q: What does the lecture say about the statistics of wave periods?
options: There is no substantiated universal distribution function as there is for wave heights
Periods vary in a narrower range than wave heights (about 0.5–2.0 T<sub>m</sub>)
Swell and wind waves overlap, which complicates the analysis
A Rayleigh distribution is often proposed for swell
Periods follow exactly the same Rayleigh distribution as the wave heights
questions.why: No universal law exists; the distribution is narrower than for heights; the overlap of swell (T<sub>mD</sub>) and wind sea (T<sub>mw</sub>) is the core problem; and for swell alone P(T) = exp(−π/4·(T/T<sub>m</sub>)²) is often proposed.

questions.q: Complete the approximate period relations.
questions.text: Roughly, T<sub>max</sub> ≈ T<sub>1/10</sub> ≈ T<sub>1/3</sub> = {{}} · T<sub>m</sub>. For the JONSWAP peak enhancement γ = 3.3 the mean period is T<sub>m</sub> = {{}} · T<sub>p</sub>, and for γ = 20 it is T<sub>m</sub> = {{}} · T<sub>p</sub>.
questions.why: T<sub>1/3</sub> ≈ 1.2·T<sub>m</sub>; T<sub>m</sub> = 0.8·T<sub>p</sub> for γ = 3.3 and 0.9·T<sub>p</sub> for γ = 20 — the sharper the spectral peak, the closer the mean period moves to the peak period. All relations depend strongly on the spectral shape.

questions.src: L4 · Important Parameters of a Wave Spectrum
questions.q: How is the n-th spectral moment defined?
options: m<sub>n</sub> = ∫₀<sup>∞</sup> S(f)·f<sup>n</sup> df
m<sub>n</sub> = ∫₀<sup>∞</sup> S(f)<sup>n</sup> df
m<sub>n</sub> = ∫₀<sup>∞</sup> S(f)/f<sup>n</sup> df
m<sub>n</sub> = (∫₀<sup>∞</sup> S(f) df)<sup>n</sup>
questions.why: m<sub>n</sub> = ∫S(f)·f<sup>n</sup>df. The zeroth moment m₀ is the variance of the water level oscillation, which is why H<sub>m0</sub> = 4√m₀; the higher moments give the period and shape parameters.

questions.src: L4 · Important Parameters of a Wave Spectrum
questions.q: Assign each spectral parameter to its definition.
pairs: 1/f<sub>p</sub>, the period of the spectral peak
m₀/m₁ — counterpart of the mean period T<sub>m</sub>
√(m₀/m₂) — counterpart of the zero-down-crossing period T̄<sub>z</sub>
m₋₁/m₀ — the period describing the wave power per metre of coastline
questions.why: The moment-based periods each mirror a time-domain quantity. T<sub>m−1,0</sub> weights the long waves most and is therefore the period used for wave power (kW/m) and, in modern practice, for run-up and overtopping.

questions.q: Sort the spectra by the water depth they were developed for.
questions.why: Deep-water spectra come out of decades of oceanography; the shallow-water TMA spectrum is a comparatively new coastal-engineering field with less experience. TMA = Texel, MARSEN (Marine Remote Sensing Experiment North Sea) and ARSLOE — the three data sets it is built on. JONSWAP = JOint North Sea WAve Project.

questions.q: The theoretical spectra are built on top of one another. Put them in the order in which the lecture derives them.
items: Phillips (1958): the descending branch S<sub>p</sub>(f) = K<sub>p</sub>·f⁻⁵
Pierson-Moskowitz (1962): adds the ascending branch and the cap, S<sub>PM</sub> = S<sub>p</sub>·Φ<sub>PM</sub>
JONSWAP (1973): adds the peak enhancement, S<sub>J</sub> = S<sub>PM</sub>·Φ<sub>J</sub>
TMA: adds the depth-dependent Kitaigorodskii factor, S<sub>TMA</sub> = S<sub>J</sub>·φ<sub>K</sub>
questions.why: Each step multiplies the previous spectrum by one more shape factor: Phillips fixes the high-frequency tail (f⁻⁵, α = 8.1·10⁻³), PM cuts it off below the peak, JONSWAP sharpens the peak for a fetch-limited sea, TMA bends the whole thing down for finite depth.

questions.q: Complete the JONSWAP shape parameters.
questions.text: The peak enhancement factor ranges from 1 to 7 with a mean value of γ = {{}} . The form parameter is σ = {{}} for f < f<sub>p</sub> and σ = {{}} for f > f<sub>p</sub>. For γ = 1 the JONSWAP spectrum reduces to the {{}} spectrum.
questions.why: γ = S<sub>J,max</sub>/S<sub>PM,max</sub> = 1…7, mean 3.3. σ = 0.07 below and 0.09 above the peak. γ = 1 removes the enhancement entirely, leaving the PM spectrum — the fully developed case.

questions.src: L4 · Determining Wave Parameters from a PM Spectrum
questions.q: Why do neither the fetch length F nor the wind duration t appear in the PM spectrum?
options: Because it applies to the fully developed sea state
Because it was derived for shallow water, where fetch is irrelevant
Because the fetch is implicitly contained in the Phillips constant α
Because it describes swell only, which has left its generating area
questions.why: PM describes the fully developed sea state: the wind has blown long enough and over a long enough fetch that the sea no longer grows, so only the wind speed U matters. JONSWAP, by contrast, makes α, γ and fp functions of U and F precisely because it describes a not fully developed sea.

questions.src: L4 · Determining Wave Parameters from a PM Spectrum
questions.q: Assign each PM relation (U = U₁₀) to what it gives.
pairs: Significant wave height of the fully developed sea
Peak period of the fully developed sea
Direct link between wave height and peak period (H in m, T in s)
Phillips constant in the f⁻⁵ tail
questions.why: The first two follow from Ochi (1982) with U at 10 m above sea level; combining them eliminates U and gives H<sub>m0</sub> = 0.04·T<sub>p</sub>². Note the original PM formulation uses U at z = 19.5 m, roughly 5–10 % higher than U₁₀.

questions.src: L4 · Determining Wave Parameters from a JONSWAP Spectrum
questions.q: In the JONSWAP spectrum, α and γ are made functions of which dimensionless group (Mitsuyasu et al., 1980)?
options: g·F/U², the dimensionless fetch
U²/(g·h), the wind Froude number
H<sub>s</sub>/L₀, the wave steepness
2πh/L, the relative depth
questions.why: α = 0.076·(gF/U²)⁻⁰·²² and γ = 7·(gF/U²)⁻⁰·¹⁴³, with F the fetch and U = U₁₀. As the fetch grows the sea approaches full development: α and γ both decrease, and the spectrum flattens towards PM.

questions.q: Sort the requirements, advantages and disadvantages to the right spectrum.
items: Requires a stationary case and an unlimited fetch
Gives too high wave periods and no H<sub>max</sub> in a storm
Applies to the not fully developed sea state; H<sub>max</sub> in a storm is determinable
Experience almost exclusively from the North Sea
Takes shallow water effects into account
Only valid at nearly constant water depth; development not completed
questions.why: The selection chart: analyse the local data, then pick PM (fully developed, deep), JONSWAP (fetch-limited, deep) or TMA (shallow). JONSWAP is a two-parameter spectrum (γ, f<sub>p</sub>); TMA still lacks practical formulas and diagrams.

questions.q: What does the Kitaigorodskii factor φ<sub>K</sub> do in the TMA spectrum, and what is its deep-water limit?
options: It deforms the JONSWAP spectrum for finite water depth and tends to 1.0 as h → ∞
It sharpens the spectral peak and tends to 3.3 as h → ∞
It converts frequency into wave number and tends to 2π as h → ∞
It corrects for the directional spreading and tends to 0 as h → ∞
questions.why: S<sub>TMA</sub>(f) = S<sub>J</sub>(f)·φ<sub>K</sub>(ω<sub>h</sub>) with ω<sub>h</sub> = 2πf·√(h/g). For h → ∞, φ<sub>K</sub> → 1.0 and the TMA spectrum falls back onto JONSWAP — the depth correction simply switches itself off in deep water.

questions.src: L4 · Information from a Wave Spectrum
questions.q: A measured spectrum shows two clear peaks, one at f<sub>p,1</sub> = 0.05 s⁻¹ and one at f<sub>p,2</sub> = 0.1 s⁻¹. What does that indicate?
options: Swell (T<sub>p,1</sub> = 20 s) superimposed on locally generated wind waves (T<sub>p,2</sub> = 10 s)
A single wind sea that is about to break
A measurement error, since a spectrum can have only one peak
A tidal signal superimposed on the sea state
questions.why: A two-peaked spectrum separates the long swell arriving from a distant storm from the short waves generated by the local wind. The same slide shows the other two-peak cases: energy transfer over a reef, and tied long-periodic waves within a sea state.

questions.q: Why are theoretical spectra used at all instead of a measured one?
options: Because in practice there is rarely enough data at the planning location to derive a representative spectrum
Because measured spectra are not allowed in design codes
Because measured spectra cannot be integrated to give m₀
Because theoretical spectra are always more conservative
questions.why: The problem stated on the slide: seldom enough data exist at the planning location. The alternative is to choose the theoretical spectrum that best fits the local conditions, and then read H<sub>m0</sub> = 4√m₀, T<sub>p</sub> = 1/f<sub>p</sub> and the Rayleigh-derived heights from it.

questions.src: L4 · Numerical Sea State Calculations, Scenario 1
questions.q: Which boundary conditions define Scenario 1 of the numerical sea state calculation (Altenbruch)?
questions.answer:
Topography: actual state of planning. Water level: 5.9 mNN (design water level Altenbruch).

Wave parameters: Hs = 3.5 m, Tp = 9.0 s, direction of wave attack θ = 315°, spreading s = 10.

Wind parameters: U₁₀ = 20 m/s from 315°.
questions.why: A numerical sea state model needs a bathymetry, a water level, the offshore sea state (height, period, direction, directional spreading) and the wind field. The profile plots then show how H<sub>s</sub> and T<sub>m</sub> decay across the shallow foreshore.

questions.q: A record of about 1000 waves has H<sub>s</sub> = 5.0 m. Which set of values follows from the Rayleigh distribution?
options: H<sub>m</sub> ≈ 3.2 m, H<sub>1/10</sub> ≈ 6.4 m, H<sub>max</sub> ≈ 9.3 m
H<sub>m</sub> ≈ 5.0 m, H<sub>1/10</sub> ≈ 5.6 m, H<sub>max</sub> ≈ 6.5 m
H<sub>m</sub> ≈ 6.4 m, H<sub>1/10</sub> ≈ 3.2 m, H<sub>max</sub> ≈ 9.3 m
H<sub>m</sub> ≈ 2.5 m, H<sub>1/10</sub> ≈ 5.0 m, H<sub>max</sub> ≈ 10.0 m
questions.why: 0.63·5 = 3.15 m, 1.27·5 = 6.35 m, 1.86·5 = 9.3 m. The highest wave of a storm is nearly twice the significant height — the number that matters for a monolithic structure or a ship.

questions.q: Using P(H < H<sub>s</sub>) = 1 − exp(−2·(H/H<sub>s</sub>)²), what fraction of the waves exceeds 2·H<sub>s</sub>?
options: About 0.03 % (e⁻⁸)
About 3 % (e⁻²)
About 13.5 % (e⁻²)
About 25 %
questions.why: 1 − P = exp(−2·2²) = e⁻⁸ ≈ 3.4·10⁻⁴, i.e. roughly one wave in 3000. For H = H<sub>s</sub> the same formula gives e⁻² ≈ 13.5 %.

questions.q: A measured spectrum has m₀ = 0.25 m². What is H<sub>m0</sub>?
questions.why: H<sub>m0</sub> = 4·√m₀ = 4·0.5 = 2.0 m. Since H<sub>m0</sub> ≈ 1.05·H<sub>s</sub>, the corresponding time-domain significant height would be about 1.9 m.

questions.q: A fully developed sea state has a peak period of T<sub>p</sub> = 10 s. Which significant wave height follows from the PM relation H<sub>m0</sub> = 0.04·T<sub>p</sub>²?
questions.why: 0.04·10² = 4.0 m (H in m, T in s). Cross-check with the wind: T<sub>p</sub> = 2πU/(0.877·g) gives U ≈ 13.7 m/s, and H<sub>m0</sub> = 0.21·U²/g ≈ 4.0 m — the two PM relations are consistent.

questions.q: A wind of U₁₀ = 20 m/s blows over an unlimited fetch until the sea is fully developed. Which H<sub>m0</sub> and T<sub>p</sub> follow from the PM relations?
options: H<sub>m0</sub> ≈ 8.6 m, T<sub>p</sub> ≈ 14.6 s
H<sub>m0</sub> ≈ 4.3 m, T<sub>p</sub> ≈ 7.3 s
H<sub>m0</sub> ≈ 8.6 m, T<sub>p</sub> ≈ 7.3 s
H<sub>m0</sub> ≈ 2.1 m, T<sub>p</sub> ≈ 14.6 s
questions.why: Hm0 = 0.21·U²/g = 0.21·400/9.81 = 8.6 m and Tp = 2π·20/(0.877·9.81) = 14.6 s. Note this is the fully developed limit: with a limited fetch, JONSWAP would give a lower, steeper sea.

questions.q: The same wind blows, but the fetch F is short. How do α and γ of the JONSWAP spectrum behave compared with a long fetch?
options: Both are larger, because α ∝ (gF/U²)<sup>−0.22</sup> and γ ∝ (gF/U²)<sup>−0.143</sup>
Both are smaller, because both exponents are positive
α grows and γ shrinks
Neither depends on the fetch
questions.why: Both exponents are negative, so a short fetch (small gF/U²) gives large α and large γ — a young, steep sea with a sharp spectral peak. As the fetch grows, γ falls towards 1 and the spectrum approaches the fully developed PM shape.

questions.q: Which statistical distribution describes the wave heights of a natural sea state?
questions.why: The Rayleigh distribution — single-parametric, so H<sub>s</sub> alone fixes the whole height distribution (Longuet-Higgins, 1952). The Gaussian distribution fails because wave heights cannot be negative or grow arbitrarily, and the phases are interdependent.

questions.q: What causes the tides?
options: The gravity of the moon and the sun
The rotation of the earth alone
The prevailing westerly winds over the oceans
Density differences between warm and cold water masses
questions.why: The tides occur due to the gravity of the moon and the sun — more precisely, from the difference between the gravitational attraction of the celestial bodies and the local centrifugal force of the rotating two-body system.

questions.q: Assign each tidal theory to its author and its content.
pairs: Newton — tide-generating forces from attraction and centrifugal force on a uniformly water-covered earth
Laplace — the tide as a sum of partial oscillations η = Σ a<sub>i</sub>·cos(ω<sub>i</sub>t + Φ<sub>i</sub>)
questions.why: Newton explains why there is a tide; Laplace gives a method that actually reproduces the tide at a real location, because amplitudes and phases are fitted to measurements and therefore absorb topography and resonance.

questions.src: L5 · Theory of Equilibrium after Newton
questions.q: Which simplifications does the equilibrium theory make?
options: A uniform water coverage of the earth is assumed
Dynamic effects are not considered
Friction is not considered
The earth's topography and coastal resonance are accounted for
questions.why: Uniform water cover, no dynamics, no friction. Exactly because topography and resonance are missing, the harmonic analysis after Laplace had to be established — and it is the method of importance for the complex German Bight.

questions.src: L5 · Theory of Equilibrium after Newton
questions.q: How is the tide-generating force defined in the equilibrium theory?
options: As the difference between the gravitational attraction and the local centrifugal force
As the sum of the gravitational attraction and the local centrifugal force
As the gravitational attraction of the moon alone
As the centrifugal force of the earth's own rotation
questions.why: Attraction F = G·m₁m₂/r² pulls towards the other body; the centrifugal force m₁ω²e₁ of the rotation about the common centre of mass pulls away from it. Only their difference varies over the earth's surface — which is why there are two tidal bulges, one facing the moon and one opposite.

questions.src: L5 · Theory of Equilibrium after Newton
questions.q: Assign each astronomical period to its value.
pairs: Orbit of the moon around the earth
Inclination of the earth's axis to the ecliptic
questions.why: The lunar day is the time until the moon stands above the same position on earth again — it is longer than the solar day because the moon has moved on in its orbit. That 50-minute lag is why high water shifts later each day.

questions.src: L5 · Characteristic Parameters of the Earth-Moon-Sun System
questions.q: Complete the characteristic distances.
questions.text: Mean distance moon–earth: {{}} km. Mean distance earth–sun: 1.496·10<sup>8</sup> km. The distance from the centre of the earth to the common centre of mass of the earth-moon system is e₁ = {{}} · r<sub>E</sub>.
questions.why: The barycentre of the earth-moon system lies at 0.75 earth radii from the earth's centre — i.e. inside the earth. The earth therefore wobbles around a point beneath its own surface, and that wobble supplies the centrifugal part of the tide-generating force.

questions.src: L5 · Formation of Spring and Neap Tides
questions.q: Sort the lunar phases into the tide they produce.
questions.why: At new and full moon, sun and moon are aligned and their tidal forces add up — spring tide. At the quarters they stand at 90° and partly cancel — neap tide. Two spring and two neap tides therefore occur per lunar month.

questions.q: In the harmonic analysis, which quantities are known in advance and which must be determined?
options: The periods are known from astronomy; the amplitudes a<sub>i</sub> and phases Φ<sub>i</sub> are fitted by least squares
The amplitudes are known from astronomy; the periods are fitted by least squares
All three are fitted by least squares from the measured record
All three follow directly from Newton's equilibrium theory
questions.why: The periods follow from astronomical cycles (earth's rotation, lunar cycle …) and need not be redetermined. Fitting only amplitudes and phases is what makes the method robust — and lets those "harmonic constants" carry the local topography and resonance.

questions.q: Sort the partial tides into their class.
questions.why: M2 and S2 are the two big semidiurnal constituents, K1 and O1 the diurnal ones. M4 and M6 are overtides — quarter- and sixth-diurnal harmonics generated by the non-linear deformation of the tidal wave in shallow water and in estuaries.

questions.q: Which pairs of partial tides produce the spring/neap cycle and the diurnal inequality?
options: Spring/neap from the phase difference of M2 and S2; diurnal inequality from K1 and O1
Spring/neap from K1 and O1; diurnal inequality from M2 and S2
Spring/neap from M2 and M4; diurnal inequality from M6 and S2
Both come from M2 alone
questions.why: M2 (lunar) and S2 (solar) drift in and out of phase over the lunar month — that beat is the spring/neap cycle. The diurnal pair K1 and O1 makes the two high waters of one day unequal.

questions.q: How is the form factor F of the tides defined?
questions.why: F compares the diurnal amplitudes with the semidiurnal ones. A small F means the semidiurnal constituents dominate and the tide has two nearly equal high waters per day.

questions.q: Assign each range of the form factor F to the tidal form.
questions.why: The German Bight falls in the first class — two high and two low waters of nearly equal size per day. Remember the direction: a large F means diurnal, because K1 and O1 sit in the numerator.

questions.src: L5 · Harmonic Analysis in Tidal Estuaries
questions.q: By which effects is the tidal wave deformed in an estuary?
options: Lower water depths
Non-linear bottom friction
Advection of the current impulse
Occurrence of reflection
The Coriolis force of the earth's rotation
questions.why: Those four. Their interaction generates the third-, quarter-, sixth- and eighth-diurnal components on top of the diurnal and semidiurnal forms — which is exactly why the shallow-water components are a sensitive indicator when a fairway is deepened.

questions.q: Inserting u = a·sin(ωt) into the advective term u·∂u/∂x gives (a²ω/2)·sin(2ωt). What does that demonstrate?
options: The non-linear term generates a component at twice the original frequency — an overtide
The non-linear term cancels out over a tidal cycle
The advective term only shifts the phase, not the frequency
The tidal wave loses exactly half of its energy to friction
questions.why: The trigonometric identity turns a product of two M2 signals into an M4 signal. That is the mechanism behind the shallow-water components — and why analysing them validates the non-linear processes in a model, e.g. for fairway adaptations.

questions.q: The tidal wave in a river becomes asymmetric because the celerity is c = √(g(h+η)) at the crest and √(g(h−η)) at the trough. What follows?
options: The crest travels faster than the trough, so the flood limb steepens and shortens
The trough travels faster than the crest, so the flood limb flattens and lengthens
Both travel equally fast, so the wave keeps its shape
The wave breaks immediately at the estuary mouth
questions.why: The high water rides on deeper water and catches up with the low water in front of it. The flood limb becomes short and steep, the ebb limb long and gentle — and in extreme cases the steepening produces a tidal bore. Advection and dissipation modify the effect further.

questions.q: Assign each tidal water-level parameter to its meaning.
pairs: Vertical difference between tide high water and tide low water
questions.why: The water-level curve is described by its two extremes, their difference (tidal range) and the durations of rise and fall. Rise and fall are generally unequal — the asymmetry that also shows up in the current durations.

questions.src: L5 · Analysis of Tidal Parameters — Current Velocities
questions.q: What is the "capsize point" (Kentern) K<sub>f</sub> / K<sub>e</sub> in the tidal current analysis?
options: The moment the current reverses between flood and ebb — generally not coincident with high or low water
The moment of tide high water, which always coincides with slack water
The point along the estuary where the flood current stops travelling upstream
The water level at which a ship of given draught can no longer pass
questions.why: The capsize (turning) points mark the reversal of the current; the "capsize point distance" k<sub>f</sub>/k<sub>e</sub> measures their offset from high and low water. Slack water and high water coincide only in a purely standing tidal wave — in real estuaries they do not, which matters for navigation and for sediment transport.

questions.q: For which purposes does the lecture need tidal water levels and current velocities?
options: Storm tide water levels for structure design
Design, maintenance and operation of structures
Design and operation of tidal power plants
Design and maintenance of waterways and shipping lanes
Shipping and leisure activities
Calibration of the Beaufort scale
questions.why: Water levels: storm tide design levels, structures, tidal power plants, shipping, leisure. Current velocities: structures, waterways and shipping lanes, shipping. The Beaufort scale is a wind scale and has nothing to do with tidal analysis.

questions.q: A gauge records amplitudes K1 = 0.07 m, O1 = 0.05 m, M2 = 1.20 m, S2 = 0.30 m. Which tidal form does the form factor indicate?
options: F ≈ 0.08 → semidiurnal form
F ≈ 0.08 → diurnal form
F ≈ 12.5 → diurnal form
F ≈ 1.2 → mixed, predominantly semidiurnal
questions.why: F = (0.07 + 0.05)/(1.20 + 0.30) = 0.12/1.50 = 0.08, which falls in the range 0.0–0.25: a semidiurnal tide, as in the German Bight. Two nearly equal high waters per day.

questions.q: High water occurs today at 08:00. At roughly what time is the corresponding high water tomorrow?
options: About 08:50, because the lunar day lasts 24 h 50 min
About 08:00, because the tide follows the 24 h solar day
About 07:10, because the tide runs ahead of the solar day
About 20:00, because there are two high waters per day
questions.why: The tide follows the moon, and the lunar day is about 50 minutes longer than the solar day, so high water shifts roughly 50 min later each day. Over a fortnight this adds up to the spring–neap rhythm being visible at all times of day.

questions.q: Complete the German waterway network figures.
questions.text: Inland shipping lanes have a total length of about {{}} km, sea shipping lanes about {{}} km.
questions.why: 6500 km inland and 750 km sea shipping lanes. Waterways are subdivided both by wayleave (inland / marine waterway) and by maritime law (inland / sea shipping lane).

questions.q: Besides transportation, which functions of waterways does the lecture list?
options: Water drainage
Drinking and process water supply
Generation of electricity
Leisure and recreation
Fishery
Storage of dredged material
questions.why: Drainage, water supply, electricity, leisure, fishery. As a transport system the waterway is described as wide-meshed and connected, eco-friendly, cost-effective and safe with low energy consumption.

questions.q: How did the largest container ships calling at Hamburg develop between 2005 and 2015?
options: From 9,200 TEU (336.7 m, draft 15 m) to 19,224 TEU (395.4 m, draft 16 m)
From 19,224 TEU to 9,200 TEU, as ships became smaller and more numerous
From 1,400 TEU to 4,000 TEU
The size stayed constant; only the number of calls grew
questions.why: Roughly a doubling of capacity in ten years, with length growing from ~337 m to ~395 m and draft from 15 m to 16 m. This growth is the driver behind the repeated fairway deepenings — and behind their morphological side effects.

questions.q: Assign each waterway to its fairway depth.
questions.why: The Jade is the deepest German fairway (18.0 mSKN, admitting 20 m draft) — the reason the JadeWeserPort was built there as Germany's deep-water container terminal. SKN = Seekartennull, the chart datum.

questions.q: Sort each characteristic to the landform it describes.
items: Lower sediment supply from the river
Results from glaciers or from former larger rivers
Higher sediment supply from the river
questions.why: It comes down to the balance between marine energy and river sediment: much tide and little sediment drowns the valley into an estuary (Latin aestuarium, "tidal inlet of the sea"); much sediment and little tide builds a delta out into the sea.

questions.q: Put the chain of impacts of a fairway expansion in an estuary in the right order.
items: Hydraulically effective geometric change of the system
Change of the abiotic system parameters
Adaptation of the biological colonization and interconnection (the ecosystem)
questions.why: Expansion works change the geometry, the geometry changes the tidal dynamics, that changes abiotic parameters (water levels, salinity, currents, turbidity, sediment transport…), and those determine which species can settle. The ecological effect is always indirect — via the hydrodynamics.

questions.q: Which of these are named as abiotic system parameters of an estuary?
options: Tidal water levels and duration of superposition
Currents and turbulence
Sediment transport and turbidity / light climate
Salinity and density
Temperature dynamics and wave climate
Species richness of the benthic fauna
questions.why: All the physical and chemical descriptors are abiotic; species richness is the biotic response to them. The full list also includes specific water surface, tidelands, shallow waters, grain size distributions, water holding capacity and organic content.

questions.q: Put the zones of an estuary in order from the sea towards the river.
questions.why: Salt water enters from the sea and is progressively diluted; the tide, however, reaches further upstream than the salt does — hence a freshwater zone that is still tidal. The tidal limit and the limit of the flood current lie even further upstream than the salinity limit.

questions.q: Assign each salinity to the water it characterises.
questions.why: The brackish water zone is subdivided into poly-, meso- and oligohaline. The turbidity zone (the suspended-solid maximum) sits inside the brackish zone, where flocculation and deposition of silt are strongest.

questions.q: Sort the consequences by the change in headwater (upstream river) inflow that causes them.
items: Reduction of the flood period and flood current duration
Extension of the ebb period and ebb current duration
Downstream shift of the brackish water and turbidity zones
Extension of the flood period and flood current duration
Upstream shift of the brackish water and turbidity zones
questions.why: More river discharge pushes seawards: it shortens the flood, lengthens the ebb, raises the water levels (enlarging the flow profile, so tidal velocities drop), reduces the tidal range and drives the brackish and turbidity zones downstream. Less discharge does the opposite.

questions.src: L6 · Density Induced Changes in Currents
questions.q: Density stratification changes flood and ebb currents differently over the depth. Sort the effects.
items: Rise of the flood current velocity and extension of the flood current duration
Reduction of the ebb current velocity and of the ebb current duration
Reduction of the flood current velocity and of the flood current duration
Rise of the ebb current velocity and extension of the ebb current duration
questions.why: Dense salt water pushes upstream along the bed while lighter fresh water leaves at the surface — the classic estuarine circulation. Near the bed the flood dominates, which is what transports marine sediment upstream and feeds the turbidity maximum.

questions.q: What is a tidal bore?
options: The steepening of the tidal wave in a river until it forms a progressive breaking wave
A standing wave at a barrage caused by full reflection
The turbidity maximum travelling upstream with the flood current
A resonance oscillation of the whole estuary basin
questions.why: The end state of tidal asymmetry: the flood limb steepens until it becomes a breaking front that runs up the river. It needs a large tidal range and a strongly converging, shallow channel.

questions.q: Where do reflections of the tidal wave occur in estuaries?
options: At barrages in the rivers and their tributaries
At river bends and changes in the profile
At groynes and other lateral structures
At the salinity front between salt and fresh water
questions.why: Reflection needs a change in geometry: a barrage (a total reflector and an artificial tidal limit), a bend or a profile change, or lateral structures. The salinity front is a density boundary, not a geometric one.

questions.src: L6 · Impact of Construction Measures in Estuaries
questions.q: What does a barrage do to the tidal system of a river?
options: It sets an artificial tidal limit, replacing the natural one further upstream
It removes the tidal limit entirely, so the tide reaches the source
It leaves the tidal limit unchanged but raises the mean low water level
It converts the progressive tidal wave into a purely diurnal tide
questions.why: The barrage is a reflecting boundary and becomes the artificial tidal limit. The second measure discussed, fairway deepening (smoothing the river bottom), does the opposite: it lowers friction and pushes the tidal limit further upstream while raising MHW and lowering MLW.

questions.src: L6 · Development of Tidal Parameters in the River Elbe
questions.q: How did the mean tidal range in the River Elbe develop over the period shown?
options: It roughly doubled, from about 1.80 m to about 3.50 m
It roughly halved, from about 3.50 m to about 1.80 m
It stayed constant at about 2.60 m
It fell from 3.50 m to 1.80 m and then recovered
questions.why: MThw rose and MTnw fell, roughly doubling the mean tidal range from ~1.80 m to ~3.50 m. It is the textbook consequence of successive fairway deepenings: less friction, stronger reflection and a tidal wave that penetrates further and higher.

questions.src: L6 · Mechanisms of Suspended Solids Dynamics
questions.q: Which two competing quantities govern the suspended solid concentration in a tidal river?
options: Sedimentation velocity and resuspension capacity
Tidal range and fairway depth
Salinity and temperature
Wave height and wind speed
questions.why: Sedimentation velocity (a property of the particles) against resuspension capacity (a property of the flow). Both are fed by the topography of the estuary, the tidal and non-tidal currents, and the kind and composition of the suspended solids.

questions.q: How does the lecture define a storm surge?
options: Storm (severe wind, u > 80 km/h, i.e. higher than Beaufort 9) plus flood (high water levels due to wind surge)
Any high water level exceeding the mean high water by more than 1 m
A tidal wave triggered by a submarine earthquake
A resonance oscillation (seiche) of a semi-enclosed basin
questions.why: Storm + flood: high water levels caused by severe winds, in coastal areas and river mouths, on tidal as well as on tide-free coasts. The wind threshold is u > 80 km/h, above Beaufort 9. (An earthquake wave is a tsunami, not a storm surge.)

questions.src: L7 · Definition Storm Surge according to DIN 4049
questions.q: Put the three DIN 4049 storm surge classes in order of increasing peak water level.
questions.why: The classes are defined by peak level and frequency: at Cuxhaven 2.1 / 4.0 / 4.5 m a.s.l. with 10 / 0.5 / 0.05 events per year; on the Baltic 1.0 / 1.4 / 1.7 m with 2 / 0.2 / 0.05 per year. Higher class = rarer event.

questions.src: L7 · Definition Storm Surge according to DIN 4049
questions.q: Complete the DIN 4049 reference values for Cuxhaven (North Sea).
questions.text: Light storm surge: peak {{}} m a.s.l., about 10 events per year. Severe storm surge: peak {{}} m a.s.l., about 0.5 per year. Very severe storm surge: peak {{}} m a.s.l., about {{}} per year.
questions.why: These apply only to Cuxhaven — max h is location-dependent, which is exactly why the table carries that footnote. On the Baltic the same three classes sit at 1.0 / 1.4 / 1.7 m with probabilities 2 / 0.2 / 0.05 per year.

questions.src: L7 · Definition Storm Surge — Example Schleswig-Holstein
questions.q: On the Schleswig-Holstein west coast, storm surge classes are referenced to which datum, and where does a "heavy" storm surge start?
options: Above MHW; heavy from > 3.5 m above MHW
Above NN; heavy from > 2.5 m above NN
Above MLW; heavy from > 3.5 m above MLW
Above the design water level; heavy from > 1.5 m above it
questions.why: West coast (tidal North Sea): 1.5–2.5 / 2.5–3.5 / > 3.5 m above MHW. East coast (near tide-free Baltic): 1.5–2.0 / 2.0–2.5 / > 2.5 m above NN. On a tidal coast the surge is measured above the tide, on a tide-free coast above the datum.

questions.src: L7 · Physical Processes of Storm Surge Formation
questions.q: Which physical processes form a storm surge?
options: Meteorological influences
Astronomical tides
External surges
Headwater influence
Submarine landslides
questions.why: Meteorology (wind and air pressure), the astronomical tide it rides on, external surges travelling in from the open ocean, and — in estuaries — the river discharge. Landslides generate tsunamis, a different phenomenon.

questions.src: L7 · Physical Processes of Storm Surge Formation
questions.q: Sort the influencing factors by their time scale.
items: Secular sea level rise and land subsidence
questions.why: The measurable storm tide curve = predictable astronomical tide + hard-to-predict "meteorological tide". Of the short-term factors the wind surge dominates; the long-term factors shift the baseline on which every future surge sits.

questions.q: How is the wind surge curve obtained?
options: Storm tidal curve minus mean (calculated astronomical) tidal curve
Storm tidal curve minus the design water level
Mean tidal curve minus mean low water
The envelope of the highest water levels of the last 100 years
questions.why: Subtracting the predictable astronomical tide from the measured storm tide isolates the meteorological contribution; max Δh is the peak wind surge. Its timing relative to high water decides how bad the event becomes.

questions.q: The wind surge depends on which quantities?
options: Fetch length
Wind speed
Water depth
Sediment grain size
Tidal form factor F
questions.why: a ≈ k·(ρL/ρW)·(LW/(g·D))·v² — the set-up grows with the square of the wind speed and with the fetch, and falls with water depth. That last dependence is why a deepening of the fairway reduces the wind set-up (a₁₀ > a₁₅ on the slide).

questions.q: How do Baltic storm surges differ characteristically from North Sea storm surges?
options: Baltic surges are marked by very long residence times, North Sea surges by very high peak levels in the German Bight
Baltic surges are marked by very high peaks, North Sea surges by long residence times
Baltic surges occur only in summer, North Sea surges only in winter
Baltic surges are purely tidal, North Sea surges purely meteorological
questions.why: The Baltic is nearly tide-free but nearly enclosed, so water piled up by the wind drains slowly — the load lasts for a long time (residence time ΔH over Δt). The North Sea funnels water into the German Bight, producing very high but shorter peaks.

questions.q: What meteorological constellation produces North Sea storm surges, and where do westerly winds raise the water?
options: An air pressure difference between a high over southern Europe and a low over the North Atlantic; westerly winds raise levels on the eastern North and Baltic Sea coasts
A high over Scandinavia and a low over Africa; westerly winds raise levels on the western coasts
Uniform air pressure and purely tidal forcing; wind direction is irrelevant
An easterly gale over the Baltic, which raises levels in the German Bight
questions.why: The pressure gradient between a southern-European high and a North Atlantic low drives the westerlies; they push water eastwards, so the eastern shores (German Bight, western Baltic coast) get the surge.

questions.src: L7 · Storm Paths of Important Cyclones
questions.q: Assign each storm track type (after Petersen / Rohde 1991) to its description.
pairs: Low forms over Newfoundland, moves over England into the North Sea, then east/southeast across Jutland
Crosses the North Sea and the Skagerrak from west-northwest to east-southeast
Forms over Greenland and Iceland and moves southeast over the North Sea
questions.why: Named after where the track goes. The famous events fit the scheme: 03.01.1976 (Jutland), 10.10.1926 (Skagerrak), 17.02.1962 — the Hamburg flood — (Scandinavian type).

questions.src: L7 · Determination of Stormtide Water Levels for Dike Design
questions.q: The comparative value method (a-b-c-d method) builds the design crest level from separate components. Assign each letter.
questions.why: The components are stacked from the tide upwards: mean high water, spring tide increment, wind surge, secular rise, wave run-up — plus a safety margin on top. Adding them separately makes each assumption visible and revisable.

questions.q: Assign each German coastal state to the method it uses for design water levels.
pairs: Storm surge of 12–13 February 1872 plus sea level rise
questions.why: Three quite different philosophies: build the level up from its components (single/comparative value), extrapolate it statistically, or take the historical worst case and add the expected rise. The three methods give unequal results, which is part of why design levels are uncertain.

questions.src: L7 · Difficulty of the Determination of Design Water Levels
questions.q: Why is the statistical prediction of extreme water levels difficult?
options: Too few data — statistical prediction of very rare events is barely supported
Data quality: morphological changes, construction measures and gauge relocations make records inconsistent
Different prediction methods give unequal results and cannot be verified
Many influences act at once (wind, air pressure, tides, external surges, headwater, climate, topography)
Because the Rayleigh distribution is not applicable to water levels
questions.why: The four boxes of the slide: influences, amount of data, prediction methods, data quality. The Hoek van Holland example shows a 95 % confidence band of about 4 m at an exceedance probability of 10⁻⁴ — the uncertainty is of the same order as the design value itself.

questions.src: L7 · Max. Water Level Gauge Delfzijl at x- and y-shift of the Wind Fields
questions.q: Shifting the modelled wind field by ±80 to 240 km changes the peak water level at Delfzijl by how much?
options: By about +1.05 m to +1.35 m, and by −1.7 m for a shift in the other direction
By less than ±0.1 m, so the position of the wind field is uncritical
Only in the timing, not in the magnitude of the peak
By a constant +0.5 m regardless of the direction of the shift
questions.why: dH = +1.05 m at dx = +80 km, +1.35 m at dx = +240 km, −1.7 m at dx = −160 km. A modest error in the predicted track of the low therefore shifts the peak level by more than a metre — a major source of forecast uncertainty.

questions.src: L7 · Storm Surge Water Level (HHW) and Design Water Levels (BHW)
questions.q: In the EAK (2002) table, how does the design water level BHW relate to the highest observed storm surge level HHW?
options: BHW lies above HHW at every gauge listed
BHW equals HHW at every gauge listed
BHW lies below HHW, since the historical maximum is treated as an outlier
There is no systematic relation between the two
questions.why: At every gauge BHW > HHW — e.g. Brunsbüttel HHW 541 cm (1976) against BHW 619 cm, Norderney 406 cm against 498 cm. The design level deliberately exceeds anything yet observed, because the record is short and sea level is rising.

questions.q: The wind speed over a shallow shelf doubles, with fetch and depth unchanged. What happens to the wind set-up?
options: It roughly quadruples, since the set-up scales with v²
It roughly doubles, since the set-up scales linearly with v
It stays the same, since only the fetch matters
It grows eightfold, since the set-up scales with v³
questions.why: a ≈ k·(ρ<sub>L</sub>/ρ<sub>W</sub>)·(L<sub>W</sub>/(g·D))·v². The quadratic wind dependence is why a modest increase in the forecast wind speed produces a large increase in the predicted surge level.

questions.q: A fairway is deepened from D = 10 m to D = 15 m. With the same wind, what does the slide say about the wind set-up a?
options: a₁₀ > a₁₅ — the set-up decreases, because a is inversely proportional to the water depth
a₁₀ < a₁₅ — the set-up increases with depth
a stays the same, because the wind shear force is unchanged
The set-up reverses sign
questions.why: The same wind shear force is distributed over a larger water column, so the surface slope it can maintain is smaller: a ∝ 1/D. Deepening therefore lowers the wind set-up — while it can raise the tidal high water through reduced friction.

questions.q: Which structures does the lecture list for coastal engineering?
options: Breakwaters (rubble mound and monolithic)
Dikes, seawalls and revetments
Storm surge barriers, sluices and pumping stations
Groynes and sand dunes
Offshore platforms
Wind turbine gearboxes
questions.why: The catalogue runs from wave-protection structures (breakwaters) through flood defences (dikes, barriers, sluices, pumping stations) to erosion control (groynes, dunes) and offshore structures.

questions.q: Which tasks can a breakwater have?
options: Protection of piers, harbour facilities and other structures against wave impact
Reduction of dredging in harbour entrances
Function as landing pier
Channelling and management of currents
Protection of coastal areas against wave impact or morphological change
Generation of the tidal range inside the harbour
questions.why: Those five. Note the double-edged nature of task 2: interrupting the longshore transport reduces dredging inside, but starves the downdrift coast — so lee-side erosion measures such as a bypass are needed.

questions.q: The protective effect of a breakwater rests on reflection and dissipation of wave energy. Which factors influence it?
options: Geometry of the structure in the ground plan
Geometry of the structure in the profile
Permeability of the structure
Dominant sea state parameters and water depth
The colour and surface finish of the armour units
questions.why: Plan geometry, cross-section, permeability and the local sea state / depth. The main task is to reduce wave energy and create calm water, and it is achieved by reflection plus dissipation.

questions.q: How is the incoming wave energy split at a breakwater?
options: E<sub>i</sub> = E<sub>R</sub> + E<sub>D</sub> + E<sub>T</sub>, giving 1 = χ<sub>R</sub>² + χ<sub>D</sub>² + χ<sub>T</sub>²
E<sub>i</sub> = E<sub>R</sub> + E<sub>T</sub>, since a breakwater does not dissipate energy
E<sub>i</sub> = E<sub>D</sub> only, since all energy is converted into heat
E<sub>i</sub> = E<sub>R</sub> − E<sub>D</sub> − E<sub>T</sub>
questions.why: Reflected + dissipated + transmitted. Dividing by E<sub>i</sub> and using E = ⅛ρgH² turns the energy balance into a balance of squared height ratios χ<sub>R</sub> = H<sub>R</sub>/H<sub>i</sub>, χ<sub>D</sub> = H<sub>D</sub>/H<sub>i</sub>, χ<sub>T</sub> = H<sub>T</sub>/H<sub>i</sub>.

questions.q: The hydraulic efficiency is R = K<sub>r</sub>² + K<sub>D</sub>² = (1 − K<sub>T</sub>²). What does a high value of R mean?
options: Little energy is transmitted into the harbour — the structure works well
Much energy is transmitted into the harbour — the structure works poorly
The structure reflects nothing and dissipates nothing
The structure has failed structurally
questions.why: Everything that is reflected or dissipated is not transmitted, so R close to 1 means calm water behind. A vertical breakwater reaches R ≈ 1 over the whole period range; an underwater breakwater is far less efficient, especially for long periods.

questions.q: Assign each barrier to its reflection coefficient K<sub>r</sub> (after Oumeraci, 2010).
questions.why: The reflected energy is Kr², so a vertical caisson returns 50–90 % of the incident energy while a beach returns a few percent. High reflection makes the water in front of the structure rough and increases scour — one reason perforated caissons exist.

questions.q: Which equation describes the flow inside a dumped (porous) breakwater?
options: The Forchheimer equation I = a·u + b·u²
Darcy's law I = a·u only
The Bernoulli equation p/ρ + v²/2 + gz = const
The Exner equation ∂z<sub>b</sub>/∂t + ∂Q/∂x = 0
questions.why: At the high turbulence inside the armour, the linear Darcy term alone is not enough; the quadratic term b·u² accounts for the turbulent losses. That turbulent dissipation converts wave energy to heat even without breaking.

questions.q: Assign each breaker type at the structure to its E<sub>Z</sub> value.
questions.why: Reducing the water depth at the structure forces the waves to break, and the breaking turbulence converts wave energy into heat. The breaker type — indexed here by E<sub>Z</sub> — decides how violent that conversion, and therefore the impact load, is.

questions.q: Which are named as the most common breakwater types?
options: Rubble mound breakwater
Monolithic or caisson breakwater
Floating breakwater
Pneumatic breakwater
Breakwater with resonators
questions.why: Rubble mound, caisson and floating are the three common types. Pneumatic breakwaters, cofferdam constructions, pile breakwaters and breakwaters with resonators are listed as the further, rarer options.

questions.src: L8 · Main Types of Rubble-Mound Breakwaters
questions.q: Sort each property to the rubble-mound type it belongs to.
items: No layer structure, almost no sorting
Uses the entire yield of the quarry — no waste
Develops an equilibrium profile under wave loading
Layer structure with core material; stability from the weight of the units
Natural stone or plain concrete cubes
Stability mainly from interlocking of the units (Dolos, Tetrapod, Accropode)
questions.why: Three strategies for the same problem: let the slope reshape itself (berm), hold the units down by weight, or wedge them together. Interlocking units come as single-layer types (Accropode, Cob, Shed) and double-layer types (Dolos, Tetrapod).

questions.q: Sort the properties of rubble-mound breakwaters.
items: Function is warranted even in case of damage
Damage develops progressively rather than suddenly
Large consumption of bulk material in deep water
questions.why: The decisive advantage is the failure behaviour: a rubble mound degrades gradually and keeps working, giving warning and time to repair. A caisson, by contrast, can fail suddenly when the design sea state is exceeded.

questions.src: L8 · Structure and Construction of Rubble-Mound Breakwaters
questions.q: Why must a rubble-mound breakwater be built in several layers rather than homogeneously from large stones?
options: A homogeneous coarse structure would be too permeable — wave energy, water and sediment would pass through it
A homogeneous structure would be too heavy for the foundation
A homogeneous structure would reflect 100 % of the wave energy
Multiple layers are cheaper than one layer of the same volume
questions.why: Stones large enough to resist the wave forces leave pores large enough to let the sea through, so the structure would not fulfil its function. The answer is a fine core, filter layers of increasing grain diameter and an outer armour layer — weight increasing from the inside outwards.

questions.src: L8 · Failure Mechanisms of Rubble-Mound Breakwaters
questions.q: Which failure mechanisms of rubble-mound breakwaters does the slide show?
options: Erosion / failure of the armour stones
Failure, sliding and tilting of the crown structure
Erosion of the inner slope by wave overtopping
Erosion of berm and toe protection, scour and undermining
Filter instability, subsidence of the core and settlement of the foundation
Corrosion of the reinforcement in the armour units
questions.why: The failure picture covers the whole cross-section: armour, crown, inner slope, toe, filter and foundation, with ground seepage acting throughout. Corrosion is not among the mechanisms shown.

questions.q: Assign each engineer to their contribution.
pairs: Father of maritime engineering; the breaker parameter carries his name
Empirical armour-weight formula from the Waterways Experiment Station, Vicksburg
