Design formulas from small- and large-scale model tests, 1988
questions.why: The lineage of armour design: Iribarren's surf-similarity thinking, Hudson's single-formula weight rule, van der Meer's parameter-rich formulas that finally brought period, permeability, storm duration and allowable damage into the design.

questions.q: Which simplifications lead from the force balance on a single armour stone to the Hudson formula?
options: The flow is assumed quasi-stationary, so the inertia force is neglected, and the flow velocity is set equal to the celerity of the breaking wave w ≈ c = √(g·H<sub>s</sub>)
The drag force is neglected and only the inertia force is kept
The weight of the stone is neglected against the wave forces
The stones are assumed to be perfect spheres of equal diameter
questions.why: Quasi-stationary flow removes F<sub>M</sub>; drag and lift are then balanced against the submerged weight, and w is replaced by √(gH<sub>s</sub>). Substituting V/A by an equivalent cube length D<sub>n50</sub> gives H<sub>s</sub>/(Δ·D<sub>n50</sub>) = K, and with the slope, ≈ K·(cot α)<sup>1/3</sup>.

questions.src: L8 · Design of Cover Layers — Hudson
questions.q: In the Hudson formula W₅₀ = ρ<sub>s</sub>·g·H<sub>s</sub>³ / (K<sub>D</sub>·(ρ<sub>s</sub>/ρ<sub>w</sub> − 1)³·cot α), how does the required stone weight react to a doubling of the design wave height?
options: It increases eightfold, since W₅₀ ∝ H<sub>s</sub>³
It doubles, since W₅₀ ∝ H<sub>s</sub>
It quadruples, since W₅₀ ∝ H<sub>s</sub>²
It stays the same, since H<sub>s</sub> cancels with the slope term
questions.why: The cubic dependence is the central message of Hudson's formula — a small error in H<sub>s</sub> becomes a large error in armour weight. K<sub>D</sub> is read from tables for the slope angle, the block type and the breakwater type.

questions.q: Which limitations of the Hudson formula does the lecture list?
options: Scale effects in the K<sub>D</sub> value
The spectral shape of the sea state is not considered
Wave period and storm duration are not considered
Any damage is neglected
Assumptions must be made for permeable structures
No wave overtopping and stationary flow conditions are assumed
It cannot be applied to natural stone
questions.why: All of these follow from the simplifications of the derivation. Van der Meer's formulas were developed precisely to remove them: they include wave period, permeability, number of waves and an explicit damage level.

questions.q: How is the breaker parameter ξ defined?
options: ξ = tan α / √(H<sub>s</sub>/L₀), with L₀ = g·T<sub>m</sub>²/2π
ξ = √(H<sub>s</sub>/L₀) / tan α, with L₀ = g·T<sub>m</sub>²/2π
ξ = H<sub>s</sub> / (Δ·D<sub>n50</sub>)
ξ = A<sub>E</sub> / D<sub>n50</sub>²
questions.why: Slope steepness divided by the square root of the wave steepness — the surf similarity parameter. It decides the breaker type and thereby which of the two van der Meer formulas applies: below ξ<sub>m,krit</sub> plunging (breaking) waves, above it surging (non-breaking) waves.

questions.q: Assign each range of H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> to the type of cover material it identifies.
questions.why: One dimensionless number orders the whole family of coastal slopes: the smaller the wave relative to the unit, the more monolithic the structure; the larger, the more the surface behaves like a mobile beach.

questions.q: How is the damage level S defined?
options: S = A<sub>E</sub> / D<sub>n50</sub>², the eroded area divided by the square of the nominal stone diameter
S = N<sub>od</sub> / N<sub>z</sub>, the number of displaced units divided by the number of waves
S = H<sub>s</sub> / (Δ·D<sub>n50</sub>), the stability number
S = A<sub>E</sub> / D<sub>n50</sub>, the eroded area divided by the stone diameter
questions.why: A dimensionless erosion area from the measured profile. Allowing a defined S rather than demanding "no damage" is what distinguishes van der Meer's approach from Hudson's — for concrete units the damage is instead counted as N<sub>od</sub>, the number of units moved out of the layer.

questions.src: L8 · Design Method after Van-der-Meer, deep water
questions.q: Which parameters enter the van der Meer formulas for deep water?
options: The damage level S
The notional permeability factor P
The number of waves N<sub>z</sub> in the sea state
The breaker parameter ξ<sub>m</sub>
The slope, via cot α (in the surging branch)
The reflection coefficient K<sub>r</sub>
questions.why: Plunging: H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> = 6.2·S<sup>0.2</sup>·P<sup>0.18</sup>·N<sub>z</sub><sup>−0.1</sup>·ξ<sub>m</sub><sup>−0.5</sup>. Surging: = S<sup>0.2</sup>·P<sup>−0.13</sup>·N<sub>z</sub><sup>−0.1</sup>·√(cot α)·ξ<sub>m</sub><sup>P</sup>. Note P appears with opposite sign in the two branches.

questions.src: L8 · Design Method after Van-der-Meer, shallow water
questions.q: How do the van der Meer formulas change for shallow-water conditions?
options: H<sub>s</sub> is replaced by H<sub>2%</sub> and the coefficients become 8.7 (plunging) and 1.4 (surging)
H<sub>s</sub> is replaced by H<sub>m0</sub> and the coefficients stay 6.2 and 1.0
The damage level S is dropped from the formulas
The formulas become independent of the breaker parameter
questions.why: In shallow water the height distribution is no longer Rayleigh — depth-limited breaking truncates the highest waves — so the characteristic height H<sub>2%</sub> (exceeded by 2 % of the waves) is used instead of H<sub>s</sub>, with recalibrated coefficients.

questions.q: Sort the properties of caisson breakwaters.
items: Can be used as a pier
Sensitive to settlements of the ground
Sensitive when the design sea state is exceeded — sudden failure by breaking waves
Strong wave reflection unless the front is permeable
questions.why: The mirror image of the rubble mound: little material and a clean deck, but brittle behaviour. A perforated front is the standard remedy for the reflection problem, cutting K<sub>r</sub> from 0.7–0.95 down to 0.2–0.6.

questions.q: Where are caisson breakwaters primarily used, and how are they built?
options: Primarily in Japan; prefabricated in a dry dock, floated to the site, ballasted with sand and lowered
Primarily in the Netherlands; cast in situ on a temporary sand island
Primarily in Canada; assembled from precast blocks by crane barge only
Primarily in Chile; excavated from the sea bed rock
questions.why: Japan above all, also Italy, Spain, Portugal and France. The construction sequence — prefabricate dry, float out, sink and ballast — is what makes the caisson economical in deep water where a rubble mound would need enormous volumes.

questions.src: L8 · Failure Mechanisms of Caisson Breakwaters
questions.q: Which failure mechanisms are shown for caisson breakwaters?
options: Erosion of the rubble foundation with forward tilt and settlement
Scour in the seabed with forward tilt and settlement
Push-out of base material due to rocking motion
Breakage and displacement of armour units
Failure of the shear keys between blocks and caissons, and failure of the front wall
Freezing of the ballast sand
questions.why: Caisson failure is mostly a foundation and stability problem: scour and erosion undermine it, wave-induced horizontal force and uplift push it. Overtopping adds an extra pulse on the rear and an overtopping-induced uplift.

questions.src: L8 · Which Loads Work on a Caisson?
questions.q: Which loads act on a monolithic (caisson) structure?
options: Wave-induced horizontal force
Wave-induced uplift
Additional impulse on the back side when waves overtop
Wave-overtopping-induced horizontal force and uplift
Pressure shocks from breaking waves (dynamic load)
Buoyancy of the sand ballast inside the caisson cells
questions.why: Caissons are designed above all against the impact of wave run-up on a vertical wall, which can produce pressure shocks. The slides distinguish quasi-static from dynamic loading, and show that overtopping adds loads on the crest and on the rear. The sand ballast does not lift the caisson — it is what holds it down.

questions.src: L8 · Design on Stationary Waves — Miche-Rundgren
questions.q: Which statements about the Sainflou / Miche-Rundgren design for standing waves are correct?
options: Sainflou presupposes a reflection coefficient K<sub>r</sub> = 1.0
For K<sub>r</sub> < 1.0, SPM (1984) reduces the design wave height to H<sub>Bem</sub> = (1 + K<sub>r</sub>)·H/2
Reflection coefficients below K<sub>r</sub> = 0.9 are not recommended
Miche-Rundgren usually leads to smaller compression forces than Sainflou
For H<sub>s</sub>/h<sub>s</sub> < 0.6 the seaward force of Sainflou must be multiplied by 1.3
Sainflou generally gives forces on the unsafe side
questions.why: Sainflou assumes full reflection and normally gives forces on the safe side — the last option inverts that. The one documented exception is the seaward force at Hs/hs < 0.6, which must be increased by 1.3 (Oumeraci et al., 2001a).

questions.q: Which wave height does Goda (2000) recommend as the design wave for the pressure figure of a vertical structure?
options: H = H<sub>1/250</sub>
H = H<sub>s</sub>
H = H<sub>m</sub>
H = H<sub>rms</sub>
questions.why: H<sub>1/250</sub> — far out in the tail of the distribution, because a monolithic structure can be overturned by a single exceptional wave. This is the opposite philosophy to the rubble mound, which is designed for an accumulated damage level over N<sub>z</sub> waves.

questions.q: Sort the statements about floating breakwaters.
items: Fast installation, independent of the building ground
Can be moved to another location and can serve as a berth
Usable only in moderate sea states, up to about H = 2.0 m
questions.why: A floating breakwater has no contact with the bed, so the ground is irrelevant and it can be relocated — but it only intercepts waves whose motion is confined near the surface, i.e. short ones. Flexible types dissipate energy mainly by deformation, rigid ones are pontoons or ships.

questions.q: A rubble-mound slope is made flatter, from cot α = 1.5 to cot α = 3.0, all else equal. How does the required armour weight W₅₀ change?
options: It halves, since W₅₀ ∝ 1/cot α
It doubles, since W₅₀ ∝ cot α
It falls to one eighth, since W₅₀ ∝ 1/(cot α)³
It stays the same
questions.why: cot α appears linearly in the denominator, so doubling it halves W₅₀. A flatter slope needs lighter stones but much more of them — the classic trade-off between unit size and material volume.

questions.q: Quartz armour stone has ρ<sub>S</sub> = 2650 kg/m³ in sea water of ρ<sub>W</sub> = 1025 kg/m³. What is the relative density Δ?
questions.why: Δ = ρ<sub>S</sub>/ρ<sub>W</sub> − 1 = 2650/1025 − 1 = 1.59. It is the buoyant weight that resists the wave, which is why the stability number is written H<sub>s</sub>/(Δ·D<sub>n50</sub>) and not H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> alone.

questions.q: A profile survey after a storm shows an eroded area A<sub>E</sub> = 5 m² on a slope armoured with D<sub>n50</sub> = 1.0 m. What is the damage level S?
options: S = 5 m²
questions.why: S = A<sub>E</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub>² = 5/1² = 5 — dimensionless by construction, which is what lets the same allowable damage be specified regardless of the stone size used.

questions.src: L8 · Exercise — classification of the cover layer
questions.q: A structure is designed for H<sub>s</sub> = 3.0 m with D<sub>n50</sub> = 1.5 m. Which type of cover material does H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> indicate?
options: H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> = 2 → riprap breakwater (natural or formed stones)
H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> = 2 → caisson breakwater
H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> = 0.5 → caisson breakwater
H<sub>s</sub>/D<sub>n50</sub> = 2 → sandy beach
questions.why: 3.0/1.5 = 2, which falls in the range 1–4: a riprap breakwater. Below 1 the units are so large relative to the waves that the structure behaves monolithically (caisson); above 6 the surface behaves like a mobile rockfill or beach.

questions.q: Which pairs does the lecture use to classify beaches and coasts?
options: Steep and flat coasts
Compensation and bay shores
Longitudinal and transverse coasts
Uplift and subsidence coasts
Tidal and non-tidal coasts
questions.why: Four pairs: by slope, by planform (a smoothed compensation shore vs. an indented bay shore), by the orientation of the geological structures relative to the coast, and by the vertical land movement.

questions.q: What is the difference between a beach and a coast?
options: The coast is where land meets the sea; the beach is the land area along the shoreline, a landform of loose particles resulting from wave action
The beach is where land meets the sea; the coast is only the submerged part
The two words are synonyms in coastal engineering
The coast is always sandy, the beach may also be rocky
questions.why: Coast = the boundary zone, formed jointly by waves, tides and currents. Beach = a landform of loose particles (sand, gravel, shingle, pebbles, shells, coralline algae) along that shoreline, and the result of wave action. The summary puts it as "Beach ≠ Coast".

questions.q: Which beach types does the lecture list?
options: Rocky beaches
Sandy beaches
Pebble beaches
Boulder beaches
Cave beaches
Glass beaches
Urban beaches
Seashell beaches
Glacier beaches
questions.why: All eight. The type depends on sediment, waves, tides, currents, vegetation and human interventions — which is why "urban" and "glass" beaches belong to the list just as legitimately as the natural types. "Glacier beach" is not among them.

questions.q: How does Dean's equilibrium profile describe the water depth h as a function of the cross-shore distance x?
options: h = A · x^(2/3), with the shape parameter A = 2.25·(w²/g)^(1/3)
h = x · tan β, a linear profile
h = A · ln(x), with A from the grain size
questions.why: The 2/3 power law. The shape parameter A depends on the settling velocity w of the sediment — coarser sediment settles faster, giving a larger A and a steeper profile. The linear h = x·tan β is the simpler alternative mentioned on the same slide.

questions.q: Assign each beach type to its grain diameter range.
questions.why: Everything above 2 mm counts as gravel, subdivided into granular, pebble, cobble and boulder. Rounded gravel is called shingle in the UK — hence "shingle beach".

questions.q: Which properties describe a single sediment particle?
options: Representative diameter d
Form and roundness
Density ρ<sub>s</sub> = m/V (quartz: 2,650 kg/m³)
Deformation
Settling velocity of the whole beach
questions.why: Diameter, form, roundness, deformation and density. Quartz has ρ<sub>s</sub> = 2,650 kg/m³, the value behind the relative density Δ = ρ<sub>s</sub>/ρ<sub>w</sub> − 1 ≈ 1.65 used in nearly every sediment formula.

questions.q: Whose diagram describes the start of sediment motion, and which quantities does it plot?
options: Albert Shields (ca. 1936) — dimensionless shear stress against the particle Reynolds number, separating motion from no motion
Robert Hudson (1959) — stone weight against slope angle
Jentsje van der Meer (1988) — damage level against breaker parameter
Christiaan Huygens (1678) — wave celerity against depth
questions.why: The Shields diagram: below the curve the grain stays put, above it the grain moves. Everything about sediment transport begins with whether the bed shear stress exceeds this critical threshold.

questions.q: The settling velocity v<sub>S</sub> = √(4/3 · g·d<sub>S</sub>·(ρ<sub>S</sub>−ρ<sub>W</sub>)/(C<sub>D</sub>·ρ<sub>W</sub>)) follows from which balance?
options: Gravity force − uplift force − drag force = 0
Gravity force + uplift force = drag force
Drag force − lift force = shear force
Inertia force = gravity force
questions.why: At terminal velocity the three forces are in equilibrium: G (weight) − F<sub>A</sub> (buoyancy) − W (drag) = 0. Note v<sub>S</sub> ∝ √d<sub>S</sub>: coarse grains settle fast and stay near the shore, fine grains are carried far offshore.

questions.q: Which modes of solid transport does the lecture distinguish?
options: Suspended transport
Bedload transport (near-bed transport)
"Swimming" transport
Dissolved transport of solutes
questions.why: Solid transport splits into suspended, bedload and swimming transport. Solutes are transported too, but as dissolved substances, not as solid particles.

questions.q: Which quantities enter the aeolian sediment transport rate Q<sub>s</sub>?
options: The shear velocity u* and the critical shear velocity u*<sub>t</sub>, as (u* − u*<sub>t</sub>)³
The air density ρ<sub>a</sub> and gravity g
The grain diameter d₅₀ relative to a representative diameter D
A moisture coefficient m and an empirical coefficient C
The wave period T<sub>p</sub>
questions.why: Q<sub>s</sub> = C·(ρ<sub>a</sub>/g)·(d₅₀/D)·(u*−u*<sub>t</sub>)³/m, with u* from the logarithmic wind profile u = (u*/κ)·ln(z/z₀). The cubic excess-velocity law means dune growth is dominated by rare strong winds; moisture raises the threshold and shuts transport down.

questions.q: What does the lecture say about the design of sand trapping fences?
options: They vary in purpose, material, porosity, arrangement, position and height, and no general recommendations exist — only some local ones
A single international standard defines porosity and height
They must always be impermeable to be effective
They are only used in tropical mangrove coasts
questions.why: Eichmanns et al. (2021) reviewed installations internationally and found no general recommendations — practice is local and largely empirical. That is typical of nature-based measures: taylor-fit solutions, no one-for-all rule.

questions.src: L9 · Calculation of Longshore Sediment Transport
questions.q: Which quantities appear in the CERC formula (1984) for longshore transport?
options: Wave energy E at the breaker line and the group/phase velocity ratio n·c
cos α<sub>b</sub> · sin α<sub>b</sub>, with α<sub>b</sub> the angle of wave attack at breaking
Relative density s = ρ<sub>S</sub>/ρ<sub>W</sub> and porosity p
An empirical coefficient K
The tidal form factor F
questions.why: S<sub>S,x</sub> = K/(ρ<sub>W</sub>·g·(s−1)·(1−p)) · (E·n·c)<sub>b</sub> · cos α<sub>b</sub> · sin α<sub>b</sub>. The product cos α<sub>b</sub>·sin α<sub>b</sub> is maximal near α<sub>b</sub> = 45° and vanishes for perpendicular wave attack — no oblique waves, no longshore transport.

questions.q: Which equation is the Exner equation of coastal morphodynamics?
options: ∂z<sub>b</sub>/∂t + ∂Q<sub>S,x</sub>/∂x + ∂Q<sub>S,y</sub>/∂y = 0
∂z<sub>b</sub>/∂t = Q<sub>S,x</sub> + Q<sub>S,y</sub>
∂Q<sub>S,x</sub>/∂x + ∂Q<sub>S,y</sub>/∂y = ∂²z<sub>b</sub>/∂t²
I = a·u + b·u²
questions.why: Sediment mass conservation: the bed level changes only where the transport has a gradient. A large but spatially uniform transport leaves the bed untouched — the reason structures that interrupt the transport, not the transport itself, cause erosion. (The last option is the Forchheimer equation for porous flow.)

questions.q: A harbour breakwater interrupts the longshore current. Why does that create a structural coastal problem?
options: Because it creates a longshore transport gradient — accretion updrift, erosion downdrift
Because it reduces the total transport to zero along the whole coast
Because it increases the tidal range at the harbour entrance
Because it reflects the waves onto the neighbouring beach
questions.why: As Bosboom and Stive put it, engineering problems relate to transport gradients. With Qx,1 − Qx,2 > 0 there is accretion, with < 0 erosion, and only = 0 is equilibrium. The same balance holds for cross-shore transport Qy.

questions.q: Assign each nearshore current to its description.
pairs: Runs parallel to the beach inside the surf zone, driven by obliquely incident waves
Narrow, strong seaward return flow that cuts through the breaker zone and ends in a rip head
Near-bed return flow directed offshore, compensating the shoreward mass transport
questions.why: Waves push water shorewards; it has to return. It does so as a diffuse near-bed undertow and as concentrated rip currents. Together with the longshore current these form the nearshore circulation that redistributes the sediment.

questions.src: L9 · Global Hotspots of Erosion and Accretion (Luijendijk et al., 2018)
questions.q: Complete the global state of the world's sandy beaches from satellite-derived shorelines.
questions.text: {{}} % are eroding at rates exceeding 0.5 m/yr, {{}} % are accreting and {{}} % are stable.
questions.why: 24 % eroding, 28 % accreting, 48 % stable. Slightly more beach is being gained than lost globally — but the erosion hotspots concentrate where people and infrastructure are, which is what makes the 24 % the engineering problem.

questions.q: Sort each measure for beach stability into hard or soft.
questions.why: Hard measures fix the position of the coast with a structure; soft measures work with the sediment budget instead — adding sand, moving it past a barrier, or draining the beach face so that swash deposits rather than erodes.

questions.q: What is the morphodynamic pattern around a single groin under oblique wave attack?
options: Accretion on the updrift side, an eddy at the tip and erosion on the downdrift side
Accretion on both sides and erosion only at the tip
Erosion on the updrift side and accretion downdrift
No change, as long as the groin reaches beyond the surf zone
questions.why: The groin blocks the longshore transport, so sediment piles up updrift and is missing downdrift. A field of groins therefore produces the characteristic zig-zag shoreline, with an accretion/erosion pair in each compartment.

questions.q: Complete the recommendation for the groin spacing a (Y<sub>min</sub> = minimum beach width, α = wave attack angle).
questions.why: a = 2·Y<sub>min</sub>·cot α. Too small a spacing wastes structures; too large a spacing lets the shoreline erode back past Y<sub>min</sub> between the groins, leaving flanking erosion and a dispersed drift at the terminal groin.

questions.q: On which factors does the required groin length depend?
options: Expected longshore transport rates
Direction of wave attack
Tidal range
Tidal currents
Width of the surf zone
Grain density of the armour stone
questions.why: All five. The lecture stresses that groins are "mainly designed based on experience": L<sub>b</sub> = f(width of surf zone x<sub>b</sub>) and a/L<sub>b</sub> = f(material, local conditions, wave direction, coastal regression).

questions.q: Which criteria are used to classify groins?
options: Function and area (beach, estuary, river)
Permeability (high / low or none)
Length with respect to the surf zone (short until / long beyond)
Height (high without overtopping / low with overtopping)
Form (straight, bended, L-, T-, Y-, zig-zag)
Structure and materials (rubble mound, concrete, wood, geotextiles, sheet piles)
Colour of the crest marking
questions.why: Six criteria. The form matters hydraulically: L-, T- and Y-shaped heads influence diffraction, while the shape also changes how rip currents form along the structure.

questions.q: Which wave processes act at an offshore breakwater?
options: Reflection at the seaward face
Transmission over and through the structure
Diffraction around both heads
Refraction over the changing depth
Reduced wave set-up in the shadow zone, producing a circular current
Total elimination of the tide behind it
questions.why: The breakwater casts a wave shadow: diffraction bends energy in from both sides, transmission and overtopping leak some through, and the resulting set-up difference between shadow and exposed zones drives a circulation that carries sediment into the lee.

questions.q: How does the ratio of breakwater length L<sub>B</sub> to distance from the shore X<sub>B</sub> control the shoreline response?
options: L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> ≥ 1 mostly produces a tombolo; L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> < 1 mostly produces a salient
L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> < 1 mostly produces a tombolo; ≥ 1 mostly a salient
The ratio has no influence; only the wave height matters
Any ratio above 0.5 produces downdrift accretion instead of erosion
questions.why: In the case statistics: for L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> < 1 there were 39 salients against 7 tombolos; for L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> ≥ 1, 22 tombolos against 18 salients. A long, close breakwater lets the shoreline grow all the way out to it — and then blocks the longshore transport entirely, causing downdrift erosion.

questions.q: How is a beach nourishment typically carried out according to the concept sketch?
options: A hopper dredger with a drag head wins the sand, transfers it and pumps it ashore through a floating pipeline
Trucks bring quarry stone that is crushed on the beach
The sand is dredged from the dune and redistributed seaward
A barge drops rock armour along the low water line
questions.why: Hopper dredger with drag head → transfer / sand silling → floating pipeline → culvert onto the beach. Nourishment is a soft measure: it adds to the sediment budget rather than fixing the shoreline, so it must be repeated.

questions.q: What impact do piers have on coastal longshore transport?
options: A low impact, because they are open structures on piles
The same blocking impact as a groin of the same length
They reverse the direction of the longshore transport
They double the transport rate by concentrating the current
questions.why: Piers stand on piles and let both water and sediment pass, so they barely interfere with the longshore transport — unlike a groin, which is a solid barrier across the same zone.

questions.q: Sort the summary statements about coastal structures.
items: Especially used under oblique wave conditions
Disturb any sediment exchange between land and sea
questions.why: Groins attack the longshore transport that oblique waves drive; offshore breakwaters attack the wave energy itself, which is what matters when the waves come in straight; a seawall stops the exchange altogether and typically steepens and starves the beach in front of it.

questions.q: How do beaches typically change with the seasons?
options: Winter storms erode the beach; summer conditions often result in accretion
Winter conditions accrete the beach; summer storms erode it
There is no seasonal signal in beach profiles
Seasonal changes occur only on gravel beaches
questions.why: Steep storm waves in winter carry sand offshore into bars; gentle summer swell pushes it back onto the beach face. The beach profile is therefore never "the" profile but a state in a cycle, which matters when a survey is used as a design baseline.

questions.src: L9 · Scales of Sediment Processes / Interaction of Processes
questions.q: Why does the lecture insist on understanding the interactions between hydrodynamics, sediment dynamics, morphodynamics and coastal structures?
options: To understand natural processes, to ensure the correct function of coastal structures, and to avoid negative impacts of human interventions
Because the individual processes cannot be measured separately
Because the Exner equation cannot be solved otherwise
Because the processes all act on exactly the same temporal and spatial scale
questions.why: Those three reasons, verbatim. And the scales are explicitly not the same: morphodynamic processes develop on very different temporal and spatial scales, from a single grain in a riverbed to a whole catchment.

questions.q: The minimum beach width is Y<sub>min</sub> = 40 m and the wave attack angle is α = 30°. What groin spacing follows from the recommendation?
options: a ≈ 46 m
a ≈ 80 m
a ≈ 23 m
questions.why: a = 2·Y<sub>min</sub>·cot α = 2·40·cot 30° = 80·1.732 ≈ 139 m. The more oblique the wave attack (larger α), the smaller cot α and the closer the groins have to stand.

questions.q: An offshore breakwater of length L<sub>B</sub> = 150 m is placed X<sub>B</sub> = 100 m from the shoreline. What shoreline response is most likely?
options: A tombolo, since L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> = 1.5 ≥ 1
A salient, since L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> = 1.5 ≥ 1
No change, since the ratio is close to 1
Sinuosity only, since the breakwater is too short
questions.why: For L<sub>B</sub>/X<sub>B</sub> ≥ 1 the case statistics show 22 tombolos against 18 salients — a tombolo is the more likely outcome. It also means the longshore transport is fully interrupted, so downdrift erosion must be expected.

questions.q: Along a stretch of coast the longshore transport entering is Q<sub>x,1</sub> = 90,000 m³/a and the transport leaving is Q<sub>x,2</sub> = 120,000 m³/a. What happens?
options: Erosion, because Q<sub>x,1</sub> − Q<sub>x,2</sub> < 0
Accretion, because more sediment leaves than enters
Equilibrium, because the difference is small compared with the transport
Nothing, unless the cross-shore transport also changes
questions.why: More sediment leaves than arrives, so the balance is negative: 30,000 m³/a are taken out of the stretch and the coast retreats. The same sign convention applies to cross-shore transport Q<sub>y</sub>.

questions.q: Two beaches follow Dean's profile h = A·x^(2/3). Beach B has coarser sediment than beach A. What follows?
options: B has the larger A and therefore the steeper profile, because A = 2.25·(w²/g)^(1/3) grows with the settling velocity
B has the smaller A and therefore the flatter profile, because coarse grains are harder to move
Both profiles are identical, since A depends only on g
The exponent changes from 2/3 to 3/2 for coarse sediment
questions.why: Coarse sediment has a larger settling velocity w, so A = 2.25·(w²/g)^(1/3) is larger and the equilibrium profile is steeper. That is why gravel beaches are steep and fine-sand beaches are flat.

questions.q: What is the sand body called that grows out from the beach and connects it to an offshore breakwater?
questions.hint: one word; its smaller form is called a salient
questions.why: A tombolo. If the shoreline bulges towards the breakwater but does not reach it, the feature is a salient instead. A tombolo means the longshore transport is fully interrupted, so downdrift erosion must be expected.

questions.q: How is an ecosystem engineer defined?
options: Any organism that creates, significantly modifies, maintains or destroys a habitat
An engineer who designs ecological coastal structures
A plant species used exclusively for dike vegetation
A model that couples hydrodynamics with ecology
questions.why: It is an organism, not a person: mangroves, dune plants, corals, reef-forming bivalves. Such organisms can strongly affect species richness and landscape-level heterogeneity — and it is exactly that habitat-building capacity that coastal engineering tries to use.

questions.q: Assign each category of ecosystem services (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment) to its examples.
pairs: Regulation of climate, regulation of flooding
questions.why: Coastal protection itself is a regulating service. The other three categories are the co-benefits that make a nature-based solution attractive beyond its protective function — and difficult to quantify in a cost-benefit analysis.

questions.src: L10 · Coastal Protection Services (Narayan et al., 2016)
questions.q: Assign each habitat to its average wave height reduction.
questions.why: Salt marshes and coral reefs are the strongest attenuators in this meta-analysis. The figures are averages over average vegetation heights, water depths and wave heights — the study itself notes that further analyses for extreme events are necessary.

questions.q: On what does the degree of wave reduction by vegetation depend?
options: Vegetation density
Habitat width
Vegetation height in relation to wave height and wave length
The reflection coefficient of the nearest seawall
questions.why: Density, width and relative height. A wide, dense, tall stand in shallow water dissipates much; the same species in deep water over a narrow strip does almost nothing — which is why habitat width is a design parameter, not a given.

questions.src: L10 · Coastal Protection Services — Morphological Influences
questions.q: Besides attenuating waves, how do coastal ecosystems act morphologically?
options: They trap and stabilise sediment
They produce organic material, which can additionally lead to soil formation
They increase the tidal range of the estuary
They dissolve the sediment chemically
questions.why: Sediment trapping and stabilisation plus organic production — which is why mangroves and marshes can accrete vertically and, to a degree, keep pace with sea level rise. That self-adaptation is the key advantage over a fixed grey structure.

questions.q: Which general requirements must be met for nature-based solutions?
options: Sufficient spatial conditions
Longer time frames, to allow for the natural dynamics of ecosystems
Societal and political acceptance and support
Interdisciplinary collaborations
A minimum tidal range of 2 m
questions.why: Space, time, acceptance and interdisciplinarity. Where space is the limiting factor, the alternative is the enhancement of grey structures — eco-engineering a seawall so that mussels, seaweed or fish can colonise it.

questions.src: L10 · Challenges — Determination of Fundamental Data
questions.q: Which fundamental data are needed to design a nature-based solution?
options: Hydro- and morphodynamics
Bathymetry
Soil properties
Climate
Salinity
Traffic volume of the nearest sea port
questions.why: All of them — and the conclusion on the slide is that this yields "taylor-fit solutions; no one-for-all solution". Every site needs its own analysis, which is one reason nature-based design is slower than picking a standard dike profile. Port traffic is not one of the fundamental data sets listed.

questions.src: L10 · Challenges — Insecurities and Knowledge Gaps
questions.q: Which knowledge gaps concerning the efficiency of nature-based solutions are named?
options: Spatial and temporal variability of ecosystems
Recovery of harmed ecosystems
Influence of climate change on ecosystems
Limits of the coastal protection function (e.g. depending on water level and tidal range)
Interaction of different ecosystems
Indirect influence of water quality
Influence of currents on wave reduction by flexible vegetation
The density of sea water
questions.why: Experience is largely based on single pilot studies, and long-term studies and monitoring programmes are lacking — hence the closing plea for collaboration between ecologists and engineers.

questions.src: L10 · Challenges — Design, Implementation and Management
questions.q: Which gaps concerning design, implementation and management does the lecture list?
options: Lacking guidance and models
Decision support tools need to be adapted
Integration of co-benefits is unresolved
Difficulty in quantifying ecosystem services
Cost-benefit analyses for grey and nature-based solutions lack data sets
Lack of suitable plant species
questions.why: The obstacle is not biology but engineering practice: without guidance documents, decision tools and comparable cost-benefit data, a designer cannot defend a nature-based option against a dike with a known design formula.

questions.q: Assign each research project to its topic.
pairs: Baltic Coastal System Analysis and Status Evaluation
Long-term establishment of seagrass ecosystems through biodegradable artificial meadows
Wave dissipation and transformation over coastal vegetation under extreme hydrodynamic loading
Aeolian sediment transport processes as a strengthening of active coastal protection
Ecologically friendly sea dikes and revetments for coastal protection
questions.why: The five projects cover the range of nature-based research: system analysis, habitat creation, extreme-load testing, dune processes, and greening the existing grey structure.

questions.q: What do the six test vegetations TV1–TV6 in the EcoDike project compare, and against which criteria?
options: Standard EAK (2002) grass mixtures against herb-rich and bee-pasture mixtures — judged on ecological value, vegetation development, dike safety and monitoring
Six different revetment block types — judged on reflection coefficient
Six sand grain sizes for dune nourishment — judged on aeolian transport rate
Six mangrove species — judged on wave attenuation
questions.why: TV1/TV2 are the EAK standard (with different grasses), TV3/TV4 add herbs, TV5/TV6 are bee pastures (own composition and ready-mix). The question is whether a more biodiverse sward can be as safe as the standard one — ecological value against dike safety.

questions.src: L10 · Definition — From Grey to Green
questions.q: How does the lecture picture the range of coastal defence options?
options: As a continuum from fully grey (engineered) through hybrid forms to fully natural
As a strict either/or choice between grey and green
As a ranking in which green solutions always outperform grey ones
As a historical sequence in which grey structures have been abandoned
questions.why: Morris et al. (2018) and Schoonees et al. (2019) are used to present a gradient from grey to natural, with hybrid "enhanced grey" solutions in between. The choice is a position on that scale, decided by space, time, acceptance and the required level of protection.

questions.q: Many terms circulate (Building with Nature, Ecosystem-based Adaptation, Nature-based Solutions…). What common objective do they share?
options: Use of natural resources and/or natural processes for socially, economically and ecologically beneficial solutions
Complete removal of all engineered structures from the coast
Maximising the reflection coefficient of the coastline
Restoring every coast to its pre-industrial state
questions.why: The terminology differs by discipline and region, but the shared core is using natural resources and processes to reach solutions that work socially, economically and ecologically at once.
